Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can you provide examples of the Beatles using their voices instead of instruments in any of their recorded songs as a group?
Answer: Listen to “I Will” from the White Album. Paul performed the entire bass part with his voice. And no, he didn’t sing that low. He sang and recorded the part while the tape ran at double speed. The tape was then slowed down to normal speed, which made his voice sound an octave lower—in the bass register.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who wrote more songs in The Beatles, Paul or John? And who wrote more songs, Ringo or George?
Answer: Every Beatles fan’s song count differs slightly, but all seem to agree that John wrote a few more songs than Paul. The Beatles recorded 13 official studio albums. Those 13 albums plus the album “Past Masters,” which includes all the songs that the Beatles recorded as singles that were not included on albums, account for all of their official, original recordings. The way I have it, John was the primary writer for 72 songs and Paul was the primary writer for 70 songs. In addition, 24 Lennon/McCartney songs can be considered as 50/50 collaborations. George wrote 22 songs that were recorded on official Beatles albums. Ringo wrote two. Both also received some songwriting credit for some fragments of songs. The Beatles recorded 24 cover songs on their “official” albums or singles. All told, that adds up to 214 songs the Beatles recorded on their official albums.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What led to the breakup of the Beatles? Did they struggle with songwriting after the release of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band? What was their final song as a group?
Answer: First, the Beatles did NOT struggle with songwriting after Sgt. Pepper’s. Their post-Sgt. Pepper’s output included Let It Be, Hey Jude, All You Need Is Love, I Am the Walrus, Blackbird, While My Guitar Gently Weeps, Here Comes the Sun, Come Together, Get Back, Two of Us, Lady Madonna, etc., In other words, many of their greatest hits. Their final song recorded as a group was “I Want You (She’s So Heavy).” All four Beatles gathered on August 20, 1969, to mix the song. That was the last time all four were together in the studio. The Beatles broke up for a number of reasons, but essentially, they didn’t get along any longer and they couldn’t agree on anything. Beatles manager Brian Epstein passed away in August, 1967. McCartney lobbied for his brother-in-law, John Eastman, as the new manager. But the others were skeptical, and they voted for Allen Klein. Klein and McCartney didn’t get along from the beginning and the final straw was when Klein forced Phil Spector’s production on the “Let It Be” album, which McCartney objected to. During the sessions for the White album all four began to assert different artistic agendas. Later, they had serious business issues. Besides the management issue, Apple Corps was a failed experiment, losing lots of money. Lennon had a new life with Yoko, which unfortunately included the use of heroin. McCartney had become overbearing, criticizing Harrison and Starr for their playing. Both Harrison and Starr briefly quit the group as a result. Harrison was frustrated with being relegated to a supporting role as a songwriter. The Beatles didn’t announce their break-up until 1970, but they had effectively broken up by August, 1969.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who was the lead singer in live performances for The Beatles?
Answer: All four Beatles sang lead at times, in concert, as well as on recordings. For example, at the Beatles’ famous concert on August 15, 1965, at Shea Stadium, the band performed 12 songs (30 minutes total). George sang lead on “Everybody’s Trying to Be My Baby” (a Carl Perkins cover). Ringo sang lead on “Act Naturally” (a Johnny Russell cover). Paul sang lead on “She’s a Woman,” “Can’t Buy Me Love” and “I’m Down.” John sang lead on “Twist and Shout” (cover), “I Feel Fine,” “Dizzy Miss Lizzy” (Larry Williams cover), “Ticket to Ride“ and “Help!” John and Paul shared the lead on “A Hard Day’s Night” and “Baby’s In Black.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Phil Spector is often blamed for his (over)production of The Long and Winding Road by The Beatles. Why doesn’t he get any credit for actually saving John Lennons lyrical masterpiece Across The Universe with a very similar arrangement?
Answer: Because Spector’s production of “Across the Universe” was just as terrible as his production of “The Long and Winding Road.” It was full of godawful angelic choruses and ridiculous Mickey Mouse strings. It ruined “Across the Universe,” which is a poetic and cosmic ballad, not music for a theme park ride. Spector’s production of “My Sweet Lord” for George was brilliant—that’s one track on which the “wall of sound” truly worked. And Spector’s production of Lennon’s “Imagine” was fine, though a bit murky. But “Across the Universe” never got a decent recording by the Beatles, which John blamed squarely on Paul.

Answer: Yes. Four #1 hits. “Get Back” (released April 1969) #1 - a slightly different version than on the album “Let It Be” “Something /Come Together” (released October 1969) #1 - from the album “Abbey Road” “Let It Be” (released March 1970) #1 - a slightly different version than on the album “Let It Be” “The Long and Winding Road” (released May 1970) #1 - from the album “Let It Be”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Two former choral musicians told me that The Beatles were terrible because their harmonies were never perfectly in pitch. How would you respond to such comments?
Answer: Generally, experienced choral singers (especially acapella choral singers) have acute hearing when it comes to pitch and can sing very well in tune. So, I’d be inclined to listen to their opinions when it comes to singing in tune. However, in this case, I’m familiar with the Beatles recordings that they’re critical of, and I must say that I don’t think the Beatles were ever “terrible” at singing in-tune. Ringo very rarely sang any harmonies. But Lennon, McCartney and Harrison acquitted themselves quite well during their Beatles careers at singing three-part harmonies in pitch. Their 9-part vocal harmonies (really three-part harmonies sung 3 times each) on “Because” from “Abbey Road” were pristine. Lennon and McCartney often sang duos where they would sing much of the song in in unison and then they’d break into two-part harmonies. Examples of such recordings are “If I Fell,” “Two of Us” and “I Want to Hold Your Hand.” Generally, Lennon and McCartney sang very much in tune. This is more impressive today because the Beatles recorded mainly in the days of fairly primitive 2 or 4-track recording technology. There was no way to fix the tuning of a note once it was on tape. Today, in the recording studio when a singer sings out of tune, one can use “Autotune.” Or one can simply “punch the note in.” Or one can adjust the pitch by looking on screen to the graphic representation of the music, finding the note that’s out of tune and moving it up or down, with the mouse. It’s easy to fudge on singing in tune with today’s technology. I suppose that if one were to go through every Beatles song the group every recorded, one might find a few tunes that were suspect or borderline in tuning quality. These would be few and far between. And one wouldn’t find that the Beatles harmonies were ever “terrible.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why was Brian Wilson, the founder and leader of the Beach Boys, such a tough taskmaster in the studio?
Answer: Judging from the videos I’ve seen of Brian Wilson working in the studio on “Good Vibrations” and “God Only Knows,” circa 1966, I wouldn’t characterize him as a tough taskmaster, at least in those instances. He seemed every efficient in the studio. He listened very intently and he was aware of very small details. But he didn’t seem to get tense. He wasn’t a difficult person—he communicated clearly. And he wasn’t particularly tough on musicians. In 1966 or so, Wilson had an easy-going, matter-of-fact manner and he communicated well to musicians what he wanted. Musicians who worked with him have generally recounted that they liked working with him. When Wilson knew what he wanted, he had a nice way of drawing it out from the musicians. I’ve seen videos of him asking the French horns to phrase a particular way, asking the bass player to pick a certain way and asking Hal Blaine, the leader of the Wrecking Crew, whom Wilson used often in the studio, to use particular sticks! In each case, Wilson got what he wanted. Basically, Wilson knew how that phrasing, that picking and those particular sticks sounded and he wanted that sound. Wilson could shape and polish a small band/orchestra performance in a short time, not through repetition, but by explaining calmly to the musicians what he wanted. The fact was that Wilson didn’t always know what he wanted. Wilson said himself that he usually only had about 1/3 of the arrangement of a song worked out before he went into the studio. The other 2/3 of the arrangement would be decided on after experimentation, which often involved having the musicians to do something unusual, using unusual instruments or trying unusual combinations of instruments. Wilson maintained a nice balance between following his written arrangements and trying out things that were experimental. “Good Vibrations” and “God Only Knows” were masterpieces of both songwriting and production.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Are there any historical songs about golden slumbers, or was this a unique creation for the Beatles' album Abbey Road?
Answer: “Golden Slumbers” was not unique to “Abbey Road.” “Golden Slumbers,” written by Paul McCartney, was based on the 1603 poem “Cradle Song” from the play “Patient Grissel.“ “Golden Slumbers” was originally a lullaby by English Elizabethan dramatist Thomas Dekker. McCartney had seen sheet music belonging to his sister Ruth for “Cradle Song” at his father’s house in Heswall, Cheshire. Unable to read music, McCartney created his own music. McCartney used several lines of Dekker’s poem with minor word changes. (Dekker’s version:) Golden Slumbers kiss your eyes. Smiles awake you when you rise. Sleep, pretty wantons, do not cry And I will sing a lullaby. (McCartney’s version:) Golden Slumbers fill your eyes. Smiles awake you when you rise. Sleep, petty darling, do not cry And I will sing a lullaby. “Abbey Road” did not credit Dekker with the stanza or with the title.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Were all instruments on every Beatles recording played by the band members themselves? If not, how can we determine which instruments were played by someone else?
Answer: Lennon, McCartney and Harrison played all the guitars on official Beatles recordings, except for Eric Clapton’s guitar on “While My Guitar Gently Weeps.” McCartney played all the electric bass parts on official Beatles recordings, with a handful played by Lennon or Harrison. Stu Sutcliffe played on a few songs on the Anthologies. Starr played all the drums set parts on official Beatles recordings, with a handful played by Paul McCartney or George Harrison. Alan White played on two of the earliest recordings. Pete Best played on a number of songs on the Anthologies. All the acoustic piano parts on Beatles recordings were played by Paul McCartney, John Lennon, George Martin or Ringo Starr. All the additional keyboards on Beatles recordings were played by the Beatles themselves or by George Martin, with the following exceptions: Billy Preston played organ on 4 songs and electric piano on 6 songs on either “Let It Be” or “Abbey Road.” Nickey Hopkins played the electric piano on the rocking version of “Revolution.” Chris Thomas, Beatles co-producer on the White Album, played Mellotron on “Bungalow Bill,” piano on “Long Long Long,” harpsichord on “Piggies” and organ and electric piano on “Savory Truffle.” As for all the orchestral instruments—strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion, etc.—those were played by studio musicians in either London or in New York City. They were generally paid the prevailing musicians union rate. In most cases, we know who played on each recording. There are some songs for which the information about all the studio musicians has been lost.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did The Who or The Beatles come first? How were they received when they first started out?
Answer: The Who wasn’t formed until 1964. By that time the Beatles were major stars and the British Invasion was in full force. The Who proved to be popular from the beginning with their singles, “I Can’t Explain” and “My Generation” in 1965. The Who made major contributions to rock music, including Pete Townshend’s use of feedback and power chords, their Marshal stacks, Keith Moon’s energetic drumming, John Entwhistle’s introduction of orchestral instruments like the French horn on stage, and Roger Daltrey’s powerful vocals. Not to mention their development of the rock opera.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What genre of music was popular in Hamburg, Germany during the time the Beatles were there?
Answer: Hamburg was a major port city and it was a wealthy city. The Beatles played stints in Hamburg from August, 1960, to December, 1962. All kinds of music were represented in Hamburg, but in the red-light, entertainment district where the Beatles played, the main influence was American rock and roll. The Beatles played long hours and catered to their audience. They played Chuck Berry tunes (“Roll Over Beethoven” and “Sweet Little Sixteen”), their version of “Twist and Shout,” “Mr. Moonlight,””A Taste of Honey,” “Besame Mucho,” “Kansas City,” “Long Tall Sally,” “Peppermint Twist,” Carl Perkins country numbers such as “Everybody’s Trying to Be My Baby” and “Matchbox” and plenty of old-fashioned American standards like “Red Sails in the Sunset” and “I Remember You.” One of the few original compositions they played then was Paul’s “I Saw Her Standing There.” The Beatles improved tremendously during their time in Hamburg and things really came together for them back in Britain in 1962.

Question: When did each member of The Beatles stop playing music professionally?
Answer: None of the Beatles ever stopped playing music professionally. John had a new album out when he was murdered in 1980. George was working on a record when he died of cancer in 2001. The record was finished by his son Dhani and Jeff Lynne and released posthumously. Ringo’s All-Star band has a busy concert line-up for the fall of 2024 and I understand that some of the dates are already sold out. Paul McCartney will never stop being a professional musician. As long as he’s able, he’ll be touring or recording.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Considering New Kids On the Block's long history on the Billboard charts, what do you think has contributed to their enduring success over almost four decades?
Answer: I saw the New Kids on the Block in 1988 when they were the opening act for the flash in the pan singer Tiffany. I was a young music critic for the Milwaukee Sentinel, a daily morning newspaper, and I saw the New Kids perform at Alpine Valley Music Theater in Elkhorn, Wisconsin. I mentioned the group in my review of Tiffany, which appeared in the paper the next morning. The concert promotor gave me front row seats, so I was very close to the stage. At the appropriate time, the New Kids on the Block came out on stage to do their opening act. There were no musicians on stage. When the music started, I thought, “Oh. They’re going to sing to tracks. Well, that’s not the worst thing.” However, when the group started singing, they were obviously lip-synching. For the remainder of their opening act, they lip-synched every single note they pretended to sing. I observed that all of the vocals were pre-recorded, including the solo parts. The in-between song patter was not lip-synched and the mics were on. The voices for that were all out-of-breath and hoarse-sounding. The contrast between the live patter and the pristine pre-recorded singing vocals just emphasized the fact that the group lip-synched all the vocals. Now, perhaps not all lip-synching is bad. For example, the Beatles once lip-synched a performance of “Hey Jude.” But it was for a television appearance (The David Frost Show), not for a live concert at a large concert venue. Whitney Houston lip-synched her famous National Anthem performance at the 1991 Super Bowl. In both the case of Houston and the case of the NKOTB, they are singers. They ought to sing. Singing should not be faked. I’m afraid that single appearance turned me off forever to the NKOTB. Above, I said that I mentioned them in my 1988 review. At the time there was still a show on television called “Puttin’ On the Hits,” which was a show in which contestants lip-synched popular songs. I suggested that the NKOTB ought to audition for the show.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who played the harmonium on "The End" by the Beatles? Was it the same song where Ringo did a vocal solo?
Answer: There was no harmonium on “The End” by the Beatles. And Ringo did not NOT have a vocal solo on it. I’ll bet you’re thinking of “Good Night,” the closing song from the White Album. Ringo was actually the only Beatle who sang or played on that track. It was just Ringo’s solo voice and an orchestra arranged by George Martin. The orchestration for “Good Night,” however, included a celesta, played by George Martin. A celesta is sometimes called a “bell-piano.” While a harmonium is a pump organ that produces sound by blowing air through reeds, a celesta is a keyboard instrument that produces sound by hammers that strike metal bars. It produces a soft, bell-like tone. It’s best known for its use in “The Nutcracker.” “The End,” by the Beatles was notable for including Ringo’s ONLY drum solo on any Beatles album.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What genre of music did the Beatles play? Who was their biggest musical influence?
Answer: What genre of music did the Beatles play? The Beatles were a ROCK band. As such, they incorporated elements of classical music, pop and country western. In fact, the Beatles crossed musical styles all the time. Their WHITE ALBUM, a double album that had 30 songs on it, is one of the most musically diverse rock albums of all time. The following styles were all represented on the White Album: folk, country rock, music hall, reggae, hard rock, heavy metal, funk, avant-garde, blues, psychedelic, and others. As far as the Beatles influences, it’s impossible to narrow it down to a single influence. Paul McCartney was clearly influenced by Little Richard, Gene Vincent and British music hall. Also, by his friend and competitor Brian Wilson. John Lennon counted Elvis, Roy Orbison and Bob Dylan among his greatest influences. George Harrison was heavily influenced by the guitar styles of Carl Perkins and Chet Atkins. Ringo Starr was also influenced by country western artists, such as Buck Owens. And frankly, the Beatles wouldn’t have existed without such earlier models as Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry and the Everly Brothers.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Were there any songs by The Beatles that had more than one writer or lyricist?
Answer: Gee. Have you ever heard of Lennon and McCartney? John Lennon and Paul McCartney were jointly credited with writing about 180 songs for the Beatles between 1962 and 1970. Unlike most songwriting teams where one person writes music and the other lyrics, Lennon and McCartney were both talented at creating BOTH music and lyrics. Sometimes the two wrote “eyeball to eyeball,” meaning they wrote the music and lyrics to a song while working in the same room, while both sang and played guitars or piano. Songs such as “I Want To Hold Your Hand” and “She Loves You” were written this way. Other songs were written by combining fragments that they had each written separately into a single composition. “A Day In the Life” was written this way, with Lennon’s verses (“I read the news today, oh boy”) combined with McCartney’s middle section (”Woke up, got out of bed”). “We Can Work It Out” had a verse by McCartney (“Try to see it my way”) and a bridge by Lennon (“Life is very short”). For most of their careers with the Beatles, Lennon and McCartney would each write most of a song on their own, and then ask the other for advice or input. Most Beatles fans know which Beatles songs were principally written by John Lennon (e.g. “A Hard Day’s Night,” “Strawberry Fields Forever” and “All You Need Is Love”) and which were principally written by Paul McCartney (e.g. “Lady Madonna,” ”Hey Jude” and “Let It Be.”) At times the second writer’s input was minimal or even non-existent. However, in most cases, both writers contributed to Lennon/McCartney songs, no matter whether the song was a true collaboration or was principally written by one writer. Thus, the answer to the question is: The majority of Beatles songs had more than one writer and lyricist.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who were the producers of "Abbey Road"? Were there multiple producers involved, similar to "Sgt. Pepper"?
Answer: “Abbey Road” was produced by longtime Beatles producer George Martin. Martin, often called the “fifth Beatle,” signed the Beatles to a recording contract and produced every official Beatles album, with the sole exception of “Let It Be,” produced by Phil Spector.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What was the most popular song performed by The Beatles at Shea Stadium?
Answer: The Beatles played at Shea Stadium two times. The first time was August 15, 1965, at the concluding concert of the band’s 1965 North American Tour. They played in front of a record-setting 55,600 people at Shea that evening. Their 12-song set included five #1 hits: “I Feel Fine,” “Ticket to Ride,” “Can’t Buy Me Love,” “A Hard Day’s Night” and “Help!” The second time the Beatles played at Shea Stadium was August 23, 1966. 11,000 of the 55,600 tickets went unsold! Their 11-song set included three #1’s: “I Feel Fine,” “Paperback Writer” and “Yesterday.” The most popular song of the songs the Beatles played at Shea Stadium was “Yesterday.” The song was performed by the Beatles as a group at Shea, instead of solo by Paul McCartney, as it was on the Beatles recording. And even though Paul had recorded the song in the key of F, the band did it in the key of G, a full step higher, forcing Paul to stretch for some of the high notes. Of course, Paul didn’t have a problem.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the worst Beatles song?
Answer: The Beatles recorded more than 200 songs on their studio albums and some of them were terrible songs. They wrote some of those terrible songs and others were covers. However, every listener will have to determine what Beatles songs were terrible and which song was “the worst” for his or herself. Good and Bad and Best and Worst, in music, especially popular music, are subjective determinations—matters of personal opinion. One thing I’ve discovered is that every Beatles song has both its detractors and its fans. “Revolution 9” (which is really a sound collage, not a “song”) is definitely the most reviled Beatles track. However, I’ve argued many times that “Revolution 9” was actually an important contribution to the music of the time. On the other hand, earlier this year, I criticized the song “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer.” Big mistake. For weeks I was inundated with mail from fans who claimed that “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer” was both a musical masterpiece and a philosophical statement of profound importance. Is it? Well, I don’t think so, but some people think so. And everyone’s entitled to their opinion.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Were there any songs by the Beatles that were considered worse than "Revolution 9" and "Strawberry Fields Forever"?
Answer: Sure. Not every Beatles song was a work of genius. There were Beatles songs that were poorly written, poorly recorded or both. Every Beatles listener has their personal favorites and, alternatively, songs that they don’t like. It’s a matter of personal taste. “Strawberry Fields Forever” is, I believe, considered by the majority of Beatles fans to be one of the band’s greatest songs. I’ve seen several rankings where “Strawberry Fields Forever” is ranked by listeners or by critics as the second greatest Beatles song (after “A Day In the Life”), ahead of “Let It Be,” “Yesterday” and “Hey Jude.” “Revolution 9”, on the other hand, is definitely the least liked Beatles track. Yet, I’ve defended it many times, and am glad to defend it here. “Revolution 9” isn’t really a ”song” at all, but a “sound collage” of random bits of sounds, conversations and music culled from the EMI tape library. As such, it was influenced by avant-garde composers such as John Cage, Karlheinz Stockhausen, Edgard Varese and Luigi Nono. It was conceived by John Lennon, with Yoko Ono and George Harrison assisting. Harrison was always interested in avant-garde music. Ringo Starr helped choose excerpts from the EMI tape library, so the only Beatle that didn’t participate was Paul. Musically, “Revolution 9” is interesting, but not great. But culturally, it was perhaps the most radical act the Beatles ever perpetuated. No one else in the history of music succeeded so well in bringing avant-garde music to millions of people.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did The Beatles actually play their own songs?
Answer: If the question is: “Did the Beatles actually play on their own recordings?” the answer is: “Yes!” All the guitar parts on the Beatles official recordings were played by Lennon, McCartney or Harrison, with one exception—Eric Clapton played guitar on the song “While My Guitar Gently Weeps.” All of the electric bass parts on Beatles recordings were played by McCartney, except for a few that were played by either Harrison or Lennon. All of the drum set parts on Beatles recordings were played by Ringo except for perhaps half a dozen that were played by McCartney and, I believe, one studio track played by Alan White. All of the keyboards on Beatles records (with very few exceptions) were played by McCartney, Lennon or Beatles producer George Martin. Both Harrison and Starr also played a few tracks on keyboards on Beatle recordings. The main exception would be the ten tracks played by Billy Preston—six on electric piano and four on Hammond organ. Also, the single version of “Revolution” featured an electric piano solo played by Nicky Hopkins. The Beatles were all multi-instrumentalists and McCartney, Lennon and Harrison all played between 15 and 20 instruments on Beatles records. The Beatles did have at least 125 studio musicians who played on their records. Generally, these were orchestra musicians from the British Musicians Union. The Beatles also had dozens of singers who sang backup on their records. I always like to point out that there are several songs on which NO Beatles played. “Eleanor Rigby,” “She’s Leaving Home” and “Good Night” were sung by Beatles, but the only instruments on those three tracks were orchestral ensembles.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who sang lead on the most songs in The Beatles? Was it always John Lennon or were there times when George Harrison also sang lead? Did Ringo Starr ever sing lead on any songs?
Answer: All four Beatles sang lead at times, but John Lennon and Paul McCartney were the main lead singers for the Beatles. Lennon and McCartney often shared lead singing duties by singing in unison or singing in close harmony throughout a song. The Beatles recorded 24 songs with shared lead vocals by Lennon and McCartney. Generally, Lennon sang lead on songs for which he was the principal songwriter and McCartney sang lead on songs for which he was the principal songwriter. Lennon was the principal writer for a few more songs than McCartney. Lennon sang lead on 72 Beatles songs and McCartney on 66. George Harrison sang lead on the 22 songs that he...

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who is credited as the writer of "I Want To Hold Your Hand"? Was it solely written by Lennon or McCartney, or was it a collaboration between the two?
Answer: “I Want to Hold Your Hand” is one of the early Lennon/McCartney songs that was written “eyeball to eyeball” and is characterized as a 50/50 collaboration between Lennon and McCartney. The two wrote it in the basement music room of Jane Asher’s parents’ house in London in the fall of 1963. Paul was playing the piano in the key of G major and both he and John were making up words and singing. According to John, Paul hit a particular chord—an E minor chord, or the vi chord in the key of G— and the song shifted into another level for the two writers. The Beatles recorded the song on Oct. 17, 1963. It was the first Beatles song that was recorded using four-track technology. The record was released in November, 1963. The single became the biggest-selling Beatles single ever and its release marked the beginning of the “British Invasion.” Lennon and McCartney sang co-lead on the song. A great deal of the song was sung in unison and the rest was sung in harmony, with Paul singing the higher notes.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who wrote the majority of The Beatles' hits? Was the songwriting credit of "Lennon-McCartney" based on an equal split of their contributions, or did one member write more than the others?
Answer: John and Paul made a deal when they were teenagers. They agreed that for any song either one of them wrote, no matter who wrote what, they would credit the song to both songwriters The “Lennon/McCartney” designation was made by someone at Northern Songs who decided that it “sounded better” than “McCartney/Lennon.” John and Paul wrote many songs together as equal collaborators, but most often one of the two was the “primary songwriter” and the other would often advice or help on the song. As far as a majority of the Beatles hits, when I look only at the U.S. Billboard charts from the time, John and Paul wrote 28 Top Ten Hits. Of these, three were 50/50 collaborations, John was the principal writer for 11 Top Ten hits and Paul was the principal writer for 14 Top Ten hits.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What was the reason for the shortened version of "Hey Jude" by The Beatles on the record and the longer version in live performances?
Answer: The Beatles NEVER performed a live version of “Hey Jude.” The clip that was shown on the David Frost Television Show in the UK and on the Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour in the US was a promotional film that was filmed in a film studio with a canned “audience.” In that clip, the Beatles played and sang to a pre-recorded music track. Some of Paul’s singing was live—his voice was the only thing that was actually live. Some of his vocal ad libs in the long fade could be heard. But all of the Beatles were either faking it or playing along with the track on their instruments. Do you think the little, beat-up studio piano that Paul used in the clip could have possibly made the rich piano tone that’s heard? No. The Beatles recording and the backing track featured the storied Bechstein grand piano that Paul had played in Trident Studios. John is shown in the clip playing an electric guitar when he played acoustic guitar on the Beatles recording. George is shown playing the six-string bass, when it was Paul who overdubbed the bass part. Ringo begins playing a part on the tambourine. When he enters on the drums—the tambourine magically keeps going. The track used for the promotional clip was exactly the same length (7:11) as the Beatles single of “Hey Jude” and the fade happened just as it did on the single. The 36-piece orchestra in white jackets in back of the Beatles was hired because of Musician’s Union rules. But the orchestra never played a note in the clip. In summary, the Beatles never played “Hey Jude” live—they played to a pre-recorded music and vocal track. The promo clip was the same length and used the same music track that was on the single.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: When did songwriting credits become evenly split between Paul McCartney and John Lennon for all of their songs, including those written together such as "Help" or "Yesterday"?
Answer: John said,” Paul and I made a deal when we were 15. There was never a legal deal between us just a deal we made when we decided to write together that we put both our names on it no matter what.” (Northern Songs, page 28) John was about a year and eight months older than Paul, so “when we were 15” probably means when Paul was 15. As far as which songwriter’s name went first, Paul was informed by someone from Northern Songs early during that publishing deal that the songs would be credited to Lennon and McCartney because “it sounded better.” (Northern Songs, page 28) By the way, “Yesterday” was written solely by Paul McCartney.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the time signature of the song "Here, There and Everywhere" by The Beatles?
Answer: “Here, There and Everywhere” is in the time signature of 4/4. The song, from the Beatles’ 1966 album “Revolver,” is a love ballad written by Paul McCartney and credited to Lennon and McCartney. McCartney ranks it as one of his personal favorites of songs he’s written. He also cites the Beach Boys’ song “God Only Knows,” which he has said is his favorite song of all time, as an influence. The song has a three-bar preamble (“To lead a better life…”) that leads into the main verse. For some reason in “The Beatles Complete Scores” these three bars are written in successive time signatures of 9/8, 7/8 and 4/4. An extra eighth note rest is added to the first bar and an eighth note rest is missing from the second bar. I find this to be an odd misjudgment in an otherwise stellar publication.

Question: How many #1 hits did The Beatles have on Billboard's Hot 100 singles chart? How does this compare to other bands with at least three members?
Answer: The Beatles had 20 #1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100, more than any other artist. Most of the artists with many #1’s have been solo artists. Question: Did the Beatles have any knowledge about computers and digital technology during their time as a band? If so, what was it?
Answer: No. Digital recording hadn’t been invented when the Beatles broke up in 1970. It didn’t become commonly used until the late 1980’s and 1990’s. And personal computers were not commonly used until the 1980’s. Even the Moog synthesizer used by the Beatles in 1969 was analog technology.

Question: Did Ringo Starr ever co-write a song with either John Lennon or George Harrison for the Beatles?
Answer: Ringo received 1/4 of the writing credit (along with John, Paul and George) for “Flying” (from “Magical Mystery Tour”) and the Beatles post-breakup singles “Now and Then” (2023) and “Free as a Bird” (1995). John and Paul gave also gave Ringo a co-writing credit on the song “What Goes On.” George helped Ringo write “Octopus’s Garden” (from “Abbey Road”). There’s a charming scene from Peter Jackson’s documentary where George becomes Ringo’s songwriting teacher on “Octopus’ Garden.” It’s a really sweet scene that shows the two Beatles’ friendship. Ultimately, George took no credit for the song, which is credited solely to Ringo, as is the only other song Ringo wrote for the Beatles — “Don’t Pass Me By” (from The White Album).

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Is "The White Album" an official title for the Beatles' self-titled double LP or just a fan term like "Abbey Road" for their last studio album?
Answer: “The White Album” is a casual fan name for the album officially entitled “The Beatles,” which was released on Nov. 22, 1968. “The Beatles” was a two-LP set that contained 30 songs. “Abbey Road” is the official name for the album released by the Beatles on Sept. 26, 1969. It was the last album recorded by the Beatles, although “Let It Be” was the last album the band completed and released in April, 1970.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who is the songwriter of "God Only Knows" by The Beach Boys and what was the inspiration behind the song?
Answer: The songwriters were Brian Wilson and Tony Asher. They wrote “God Only Knows” in 1966 for the Beach Boys “Pet Sounds” album. The song was also the B-side of the 1966 single “Wouldn’t It Be Nice.” That was the Beach Boys single just prior to “Good Vibrations.” Brian Wilson has said that Asher was fond of the standard “Stella by Starlight” and just that fact provided some of the inspiration. Wilson also has said that he was trying to out-do the Beatles “Rubber Soul,” which had recently come out. Wilson and Paul McCartney directly competed with each other in those days. They became good friends. Paul McCartney has stated unequivocally that his favorite song ever is “God Only Knows.” McCartney has said that his “Here There and Everywhere,” which was on the Beatles “Revolver” album, was his answer to Wilson’s “God Only Knows.” Another great songwriter, Jimmy Webb, has also said that “God Only Knows” is his favorite song. Webb has also stated that he believes that Brian Wilson was directly inspired by liturgical music. Besides the fact that the song is a pop song that mentions God (which was very unusual in 1966) the song is very innovative with regard to harmony. It uses lots of chords in positions other than root position and is freeform the way it kind of moves about different keys. Wilson said it was the only song he ever wrote that wasn’t in a definite key. The song also had very unusual instrumentation. Wilson produced the recording session, which included about 20 session musicians who played such instruments as sleigh bells (played by Hal Blaine), French horn, alto flute (played by Jim Horn), accordion, upright bass AND electric bass, 12-string guitar, harpsichord (played by Larry Knechtel) and tack piano. Paul McCartney has said that it is “the greatest song ever written.”

Question: Did Buddy Holly have a significant influence on The Beatles' songwriting?
Answer: Yes. The Beatles idolized Holly and performed dozens of Holly’s songs in their early days. Later, they covered Holly’s “Words of Love” on their 1964 album “Beatles for Sale.” Paul McCartney was such a Holly fan that he purchased the publishing rights to Holly’s catalog in 1973. And the Beatles chose their band name in imitation of Holly’s band The Crickets. Early on, the Beatles were strongly influenced by Holly. The Fab Four eventually grew beyond Holly’s simple pop style. But Holly probably would have, too, had he not tragically died on “The Day the Music Died”— Feb. 3, 1959— in the plane crash that also killed Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper.

Question: Did Slim Whitman really sell more records than The Beatles?
Answer: No. Slim Whitman sold about 1/10 the number of records the Beatles did. However, Whitman sold about 70 million records, which is a lot! Slim Whitman (1923–2013) was an American country music singer/songwriter/guitarist. He was best known for his yodeling and for marketing his records on television during the 1970’s and 1980’s. Whitman recorded about 100 albums and he was always more popular in Europe, especially the UK, than in America. George Harrison cited Slim Whitman as an influence on his guitar playing. Whitman played the guitar left-handed. When another left-handed guitarist named Paul McCartney bought a right-handed instrument, the future Beatle learned how to string the guitar for a left-hander by studying a photo of Whitman. Whitman’s 1955 single “Rose Marie” topped the UK charts for 11 weeks at number one. That was a UK record that stood for 36 years and it was never bested by the Beatles.

Question: Did the Beatles ever perform concerts in Russia or China (or any other country)?
Answer: The Beatles never performed in Russia or China. However, they did perform more than 800 times in 16 different countries before they quit touring in August, 1966. Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can you name any Beatles songs that have unconventional chord progressions other than I-IV-V-I?
Answer: One of the Beatles’ greatest strengths as songwriters was their ability to create chord progressions that sounded fresh, were musically interesting and went places that the listener didn’t expect. The Beatles rarely relied on I-IV-V harmonies. Even when they did a song like “I Saw Her Standing There,” which was basically a three-chord rocker, Paul McCartney added an extra chord—based on the flatted 6th degree of the scale—that put the song into a category beyond three-chord rock. All three of the main songwriters for the Beatles were adept at creating amazing chord progressions. John Lennon showed his ability with “Julia,” “If I Fell,” “Across the Universe,” “Because” and “Strawberry Fields Forever,” among others. Some of McCartney’s amazing chord progressions included “All My Loving,” “For No One,” “Here There and Everywhere,” “Penny Lane” and “Blackbird.” George Harrison was also capable of creating wonderful chord progressions—”Something” and “Here Comes the Sun” were masterful. In all three cases, it was generally the root movement of the chords that really made them interesting, not necessarily the quality of the chords. The Beatles sometimes used extended chords or altered chords, but for the most part they stuck to major and minor triads, dominant 7ths and minor 7ths. They simply used their ears as their guide to decide what chords to use.

Question: Can you name a Beatles song that was not performed by John, Paul, George, or Ringo?
Answer: No. At least one Beatle either played an instrument or sang on every Beatles song that was included on a Beatles studio album or released as a single. However, there are at least three Beatles songs on which no Beatle played an instrument. “Eleanor Rigby” featured the vocals of Paul, John and George. The only instruments on the recording were a string octet arranged by George Martin. She’s Leaving Home” featured the vocals of Paul and John. The only instruments on the recording were 10 strings and a harp, arranged by Mike Leander. “Good Night” featured the vocals of Ringo. The instrumental track was arranged by George Martin and included 19 strings, 3 flutes, clarinet, horn, vibraphone, celesta and harp. It also featured the Mike Sammes singers, a group of 9 professional backing singers.

Question: Who had the most songwriting credits on a single album in The Beatles (excluding contributions to other artists)?
Answer: Beatles songs written by Lennon and McCartney either in collaboration or principally by either one were always credited to “John Lennon and Paul McCartney.” The 1968 double album entitled “The Beatles” (“The White Album”) had 30 songs on it. 25 were credited to Lennon and McCartney. Of those, Beatles experts agree that 13 were principally written by Lennon and 12 were principally written by McCartney. Lennon thereby had the most songwriting credits by number on a single Beatles album. Lennon also had the most songwriting credits by PERCENTAGE on a single Beatles album. The 1964 “A Hard Day’s Night” album had 13 songs on it, all credited to Lennon and McCartney. It’s generally agreed that “I’m Happy Just to Dance With You” was a 50/50 collaboration. Of the others, Lennon is agreed to be principal writer of 9 and McCartney the principal writer of 3 songs. That gives McCartney 27% of the songwriting credits on “A Hard Day’s Night” and Lennon 73%. So Lennon also has the most songwriting credits by percentage on a single Beatles album.

Question: Did the Beatles ever record songs separately during their career? If so, what was the reason for this?
Answer: Yes. All four Beatles recorded songs without the assistance of the others that were included on Beatles albums. John Lennon recorded “Julia” by himself. The track featured Lennon singing and playing his acoustic guitar. Ringo recorded “Good Night” without the others. He sang lead to an orchestral track arranged by George Martin. George Harrison recorded “Without You Without You” without the other Beatles. Harrison sang vocals, and played tambura, sitar swarmandal and guitar. Five other musicians played Indian instruments and there were ten string players. Paul McCartney recorded the most Beatles songs by himself. First, McCartney sang and played his acoustic guitar, with a string quartet accompaniment, on “Yesterday.” The other Beatles didn’t participate in the recording. McCartney recorded “Blackbird,” “Wild Honey Pie” and “Her Majesty“ completely by himself. McCartney was the only Beatle who played and sang on “Mother Nature’s Son.” And he played piano, bass and drums and sang on “Martha My Dear,” while accompanied by a 14-piece orchestra. However, that piece may not actually qualify as McCartney separately because George Harrison is believed to have played guitar uncredited. Reasons why the Beatles all recorded songs separately vary. John did “Julia” by himself because it was a song about his mother and it meant something personal to him. John had written “Good Night” for Ringo to sing so Ringo sang it even though no other Beatle participated. George recorded “Within You Without You” without the other Beatles because the song required some specialization in Indian music and instrumentation, which the other Beatles didn’t have. Paul recorded “Yesterday” by himself because it was his song all the way. “Blackbird” was beautiful with just a single guitar. And the others came about because Paul was working a lot on his own. during the “White Album” sessions.

Question: Why was George Harrison not the lead guitar in Taxman?

They started over on April 21st, completing 11 takes, at which time they added the vocals. The track consisted primarily of Harrison’s distorted guitar chops on 2 and 4, McCartney’s tight bass licks and Starr’s solid drumming. Harrison sang lead and Lennon and McCartney sang backing vocals. McCartney overdubbed the scintillating guitar solo at the April 21st session. Question: Who wrote the majority of The Beatles' songs during their time as a group (excluding later singles after their breakup)?
Answer: The following answer includes the songs the Beatles recorded on their 13 studio albums and the singles released during their time as a group. 1 song by Lennon/McCartney/Harrison/Starkey (“Flying”) 1 song by Lennon/McCartney/Starkey (“What Goes On”) 2 songs by Richard Starkey (a/k/a Ringo Starr) 22 songs by George Harrison 23 cover songs by other songwriters 160 songs attributed to Lennon and McCartney Of those 160 L/M songs, Beatles experts generally agree that 18 can be considered 50/50 collaborations between Lennon and McCartney. That includes songs they wrote “eyeball to eyeball” and songs where one wrote a part of the song and the other wrote a part of the song (such as “A Day In the Life”). The other L/M songs were principally written by either Lennon or McCartney. When one principally wrote a song, the other would usually review the song and offer suggestions or touch-ups. That happened for the majority of songs but not in every case. 70 songs were principally written by McCartney. 72 songs were principally written by Lennon. Question: Who had more hits: The Rolling Stones or Paul McCartney & Wings? Why did McCartney have less hits than the Stones despite being in a more popular band (The Beatles)?

Question: What was the reason for the Beatles changing the tempo of "I'll Follow The Sun" from fast to slow?
Answer: There’s a 1960 recording on YouTube of the Beatles (or Beatles-to-be) performing “I’ll Follow the Sun” in 1960. The thing that distinguishes the recording from the version the Beatles eventually recorded in 1964 on the “Beatles For Sale” album is the FEEL, not necessarily the tempo, although the original tempo WAS a bit faster. The feel on the 1960 version is country western swing. McCartney, who wrote the song when he was 16, sang (in a lower key) and his voice sounded darker. George Harrison played his best Carl Perkins licks. Stu Sutcliffe possibly played bass. Supposedly, Paul’s brother Mike played drums. For the album version in 1964, the Beatles straightened out the feel—playing the song using straight eighths, not swing eighths. They also slowed the tempo down a tad, However, at about 132 beats per minute, it’s still a very brisk tempo for a ballad. Ringo didn’t even play drums on the 1964 track—he just tapped his knees. The change in feel and tempo made the song better, in my opinion. It helped emphasize the song’s lovely melody and chord changes.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What was the cost of popular songs when they were first published as sheet music? When did this practice begin?
Answer: Sheet music has been published since the invention of the printing press in the 1400’s. However, the popular music business essentially arose in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Stephen Foster, 1826–1864, is regarded as “America’s first professional songwriter.” Sheet music was sold for 5 or 10 cents a song in the mid-1800’s. Foster typically sold his songs outright to music publishers, for a flat fee, usually $100 or less. Foster’s 1851 composition, “Old Folks at Home” (a/k/a “Swanee River”), reputedly sold 20 million copies. Foster earned $100 on that song and he earned a grand total of $15,000 on his songs in his lifetime. In the 1890’s, ragtime became America’s music craze. The “King of Ragtime,” Scott Joplin signed a deal with a publisher that gave him a royalty of one cent (about 35 cents today) on each copy of sheet music sold. Sheet music sold for about 25 cents a song (which is about $8.79 now). A one cent royalty may not seem like much, but when Joplin’s ”Maple Leaf Rag” was published in 1899, it sold a million copies, earning Joplin about $10,000 in royalties ($350,000 today). Joplin wrote about 40 rags. By 1910, the American music business had really taken shape. Woolworths stocked a thousand titles of sheet music and sold sheets for 10 cents a copy. Irving Berlin, known as the “Father of American music,” wrote his “Alexander’s Ragtime Band” in 1911. It sold 1.5 million copies during its first year. Composers such as Jerome Kern and George Gershwin were soon to follow and the sheet music business became a major industry throughout most of the 20th Century. Today, because of a number of reasons, sheet music sales have declined. The big online sheet music distributors, Musicnotes and Sheet Music Direct, sell digital sheet music for about $5 or $6 a song.

Question: Who wrote the song "Lucy" on the Beatles' album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band? Is the song named after anyone in particular?
Answer: “Lucy In the Sky with Diamonds” was written primarily by John with help from Paul. John’s son, Julian, came home from school with a drawing he called “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds.” It depicted Julian’s classmate, Lucy O’Donnell. The letters of the nouns in the title spell “LSD.” But John always insisted that the song was not about the drug. Ringo was at John’s house the day he came home with the drawing and has confirmed the story. The lyrics are obviously inspired by Lewis Carroll. Paul contributed the phrases “newspaper taxis” and “cellophane flowers.” He also played the synth-like line done on a Lowrey organ with lots of studio effects. In his mid-forties, Julian renewed his friendship with Lucy O’Donnell before she passed away from complications of lupus.

Question: Did The Beatles have any performances after their concert at Shea Stadium? If yes, where and when did they take place?
Answer: The Beatles’ Shea Stadium concert was the band’s first date on the 1965 U.S. tour. That concert was on Aug. 15, 1965. Concerts followed in 8 American cities and one Canadian city, ending on Aug. 31st. The Beatles did a short world tour in June and July, 1966. There were three dates in West Germany, three in Tokyo and one in Manila. The Beatles’ 1966 U.S. Tour was in August. The tour began in Chicago on August 12, 1966, and ended with the 14th tour date in San Francisco’s Candlestick Park on August 29. The Beatles’ Rooftop Concert was an impromptu affair on the roof of their Apple Corps headquarters in London on Jan. 30, 1969. The temperature was 45 degrees and the winds were harsh. John borrowed Yoko’s fur coat and Ringo wore his wife Maureen’s red coat. That was the last time the band played together in public.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why did the Beatles only have four members? Could they have added a fifth member if needed?
Answer: The original line-up of the Beatles was five members. The Beatles first played under the name The Beatles in August, 1960 in Hamburg. The line-up was: John Lennon, Paul McCartney and George Harrison, all on guitar and vocals, Stu Sutcliffe on bass guitar and vocals, and Pete Best on drums. Stu Sutcliffe, in fact, was the one who invented the name BEATLES, although he initially spelled it BEATALS. Sutcliffe quit the Beatles in July, 1961, making the group a quartet. McCartney took over the bass guitar duties because he was the only one of the three guitarists who could play bass. Pete Best was fired from the Beatles on August 16, 1962, and replaced by Ringo Starr. The musician who came closest to becoming an actual fifth member of the band was Billy Preston, who played electric piano and organ on the Beatles final two albums and appeared with the group in their final live performance, the Rooftop Concert. The Beatles billed the single “Get Back” as “The Beatles with Billy Preston.” Lennon wanted the group to hire Billy permanently.
