Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Were any other members of The Beatles involved in the production of Let It Be or Abbey Road, besides Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr?
Answer: Why would anyone think that the last two Beatles albums were created by only McCartney and Starr? It’s contrary to common sense. Adding up the songs from both albums, McCartney was the main writer for 12.5 songs, Lennon for 10.5 songs, Harrison for 4 songs and Starr for one song. “Abbey Road” was released in September, 1969. The Beatles recorded it in July and August of 1969. Two of the best songs on “Abbey Road” were written by George Harrison--”Something” and “Here Comes the Sun.” John Lennon’s “Because,” featuring triple-tracked vocals by Paul, George and John. There are nine vocals beautifully stacked on that number. “Come Together” was a Lennon composition that is almost always regarded by both critics and fans as one of the top Beatles songs. Another Lennon contribution, “I Want You (She’s So Heavy),” was the last song recorded by all four Beatles in the studio together. Starr wrote and sang the charming children’s song “Octopus’ Garden.” McCartney wrote and sang “You Never Give Me Your Money,” “Golden Slumbers” and “Oh! Darling,” all great songs. The finale, “The End,” not only featured Starr’s one and only drum solo on record, but it featured the other three Beatles playing lead guitar solos. McCartney, Harrison and Lennon each play 2-bar solos, three times each, in that order on that number. “Let It Be” was released in May, 1970, but was largely recorded in 1968 and early 1969. It included two songs by George (“For You Blue” and “I Me Mine”) and Lennon’s “Across the Universe” and “One After 909.” There were two great Lennon/McCartney duets--”Two of Us” and “I’ve Got a Feeling.” And there was McCartney’s great trio of hits--”Get Back” (recorded and released as single in 1969), “Let It Be” and “The Long and Winding Road.” The latter two songs, as mixed by Phil Spector, were so disappointing to McCartney, that he eventually re-mixed the whole album and called it “Let it Be (Naked).” McCartney had the biggest hits on the last album, but both albums were group efforts with important contributions by all four Beatles.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why was "The Monkees" successful on television despite only featuring cover songs and not being as good as "The Beatles" on TV?
Answer: The Monkees’ television series had good ratings in its first year. It faded in its second year and was cancelled after two years. The Monkees were originally cast to portray a rock band on TV. Their songs were sung by the Monkees but were written by professional songwriters and played primarily by studio musicians. In actuality, the Monkees’ success as recording artists far outstripped their TV show. Their first album spent 13 weeks at #1. Their first 4 albums all went to #1. They sold 75 million records! They all had appealing personalities, which could be likened to the Beatles. Beatles George Harrison and John Lennon were acknowledged Monkees fans. The Monkees’ songs were NOT cover songs. From the beginning. they were written for the Monkees by some of the biggest songwriters of the era—Neil Diamond, Carole King, David Gates, Neil Sedaka and Tommy Boyce and Bobby Hart. Eventually, the Monkees gained control over their music, wrote most of their own material and did a great deal of the playing on their recordings. Ultimately, their success as rock stars is more important than their TV series. They were one of the most successful bands of the late 1960’s. They had five Top-3 albums and six Top-3 singles.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: If you were Paul McCartney, would you have asked around to see where "Yesterday" originated?
Answer: Paul McCartney woke up one morning early in 1965 in his room at the house of his girlfriend, Jane Asher, with the entire melody of “Yesterday” in his head. He had a piano in his room and he played the tune upon waking, The tune didn’t have any words, so he initially called it “Scrambled Eggs.” He was concerned that he might have subconsciously plagiarized the tune, so for a month or more he played the tune for anyone who would listen. The consensus of the listeners was that it was an original tune. According to an interview with McCartney in 1967, it was John Lennon who later suggested the title “Yesterday.” That fact is rarely referenced in articles about the song. McCartney acted reasonably. After all, when a person awakes with a song in his head, it’s usually a song the person heard recently, not an originally tune. McCartney thought it was possible that he had heard the song before. And he certainly didn’t expect to write an entire tune during his sleep. McCartney DID do what he could to determine that the tune was an original tune.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Was John Lennon the true rock star of the Beatles?
Answer: The Beatles had 4 true rock stars. It seems pointless to argue that one was more of a “true” rock star than the others. That being said, however, I will freely admit that John was always my personal favorite from the day I first saw the Beatles on Ed Sullivan in February, 1964. Let me recount the reasons. First, John looked the coolest and had the most swagger when he stood on stage holding his Rickenbacker guitar. Second, John was often called by journalists of the period ”the smart Beatle.” He wrote two books and published them early in the Beatles career. I read his books when they came out in 1964–1965. As a nine-year-old, I thought he was cool both to be smart and write books — the kind of rock star I liked. It seems to me that John wrote more rock anthems of the period than his Beatles cohorts. Those songs include ”All You Need Is Love,” “Give Peace a Chance” and “Imagine.” He also wrote the Beatles songs that most blew my young mind, like ”I Am the Walrus,” “Strawberry Fields Forever” and “Across the Universe.” John had one of the best pop voices ever. He could use his hard, rasping scream in songs like “Twist and Shout.” But he could also portray a softer vulnerability in such songs as “Julia” He was very politically active, especially in the anti-war movement. He was so politically active that Richard Nixon tried to have him deported from the US. He was very outspoken, sometimes getting himself in trouble, such as the time when he said the Beatles were more popular than Jesus. He rarely held back. These are some of the reasons I admired John the most of the Beatles and might argue that he was the most “true” rock star.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Which songs did George Harrison not play on the White Album?
Answer: No Beatle played on “Good Night.” It was sung by Ringo with an orchestral track. “Julia” was played and sung by John only. “Martha My Dear,” “Blackbird,” “Wild Honey Pie” and “Mother Nature’s Son” were played and sung by Paul only. Two of those also had orchestral tracks. “Why Don’t We Do It In the Road” and “Don’t Pass Me By” included only Ringo and Paul. George was a co-creator of “Revolution 9.” The sole track that the other three Beatles played on, but not George, was “I Will.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Are there multiple versions of Rhapsody In Blue?
Answer: Yes. The three main versions were all orchestrated by Ferde Grofe. The original 1924 version was for solo piano and jazz band. The band included 3 multi-reed players, 2 trumpets, 2 French horns, 2 trombones, tuba, double bass, drum set, timpani, glockenspiel, tenor banjo and 8 violins. The 1926 theater orchestra version included: solo piano, flute, oboe, 2 clarinets, bassoon, 3 saxophones, 2 French horns, 2 trumpets, two trombones and the same percussion and strings as above. The 1942 version for symphony orchestra included: solo piano, 2 flutes, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, bass clarinet, 2 alto saxes, one tenor sax, 3 French horns, 3 trumpets, 3 trombones, tuba, drums, timpani, suspended cymbal, snare drum, bass drum, tam-tam, triangle, glockenspiel, tenor banjo and a full string section.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who is the songwriter of "She Said, She Said" by The Beatles?
Answer: “She Said, She Said” was written by John Lennon with help from George Harrison. The song is attributed to Lennon and McCartney.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did The Beatles ever consider having three guitarists instead of just two (Paul and George)?
Answer: The Beatles DID have a three-guitar lineup at the beginning. When the Beatles first played Hamburg in August, 1960, their lineup was: John Lennon, guitar and vocals Paul McCartney, guitar and vocals George Harrison, guitar and vocals Pete Best, drums Stu Sutcliffe, bass. When Sutcliffe left the band in 1961, McCartney took over the bass. In 1962, Pete Best was fired and replaced by Ringo Starr. McCartney often played guitar on Beatles records. The best comparison of the three guitarists is on “The End,” the last song on the last album the Beatles recorded. Starting at about 0:53 the three Beatles guitarists trade short solos. Each play three short solos of two bars each. The order each time is Paul McCartney, George Harrison and John Lennon.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who wrote more songs on the White Album, John Lennon or Paul McCartney?
Answer: Lennon was the principal writer of 13 songs on the White Album, McCartney 12.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can you provide information on the composition of The Beatles' song "Yesterday"? Who is credited with coming up with the chord progression?
Answer: Paul McCartney is the sole author of “Yesterday,” which is credited to Lennon and McCartney. McCartney is also the only Beatle to perform on the Beatles’ recording. McCartney played acoustic guitar and sang on the record, which also includes a string quartet arranged by George Martin. McCartney dreamed the music for the song—Yes, he woke up one day with the entire melody of the song in his head. He had no lyrics or title for it, so he called it ”Scrambled Eggs” for a few months until he came up with the lyrics. McCartney is solely responsible for the chord progression, which bears a similarity to “Georgia on My Mind,” a 1930 composition by Hoagy Carmichael and Stuart Gorrell. The most famous version of “Georgia on My Mind” (or simply “Georgia”) is by Ray Charles. McCartney certainly knew the famous 1960 Charles recording.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who wrote all of The Beatles' songs and lyrics? Did any other members contribute to the songwriting process or were they all written by Lennon-McCartney?
Answer: John Lennon and Paul McCartney were the main songwriters for the Beatles. More than 75% of the songs the Beatles recorded on the Beatles’ ”official” albums and singles were credited to Lennon and McCartney. However, George Harrison wrote 22 Beatles songs and Ringo Starr wrote 2 Beatles songs by himself. And both were credited with portions of other songs. The Beatles also recorded 23 covers on their official albums, written by Chuck Berry, Buddy Holly, and even Burt Bacharach and Carole King. Of the 160 songs credited to Lennon and McCartney, Beatles scholars say that only about 18 songs should be considered 50/50 collaborations. Of the other songs, scholars identify the songs on which Paul was the primary songwriter and the songs on which John Lennon was the primary songwriter. Lennon has a slight edge over McCartney in that number. However, plenty of evidence indicates that Lennon and McCartney’s songwriting process was sometimes a group effort and that both Harrison and Starr made significant contributions to Lennon/McCartney songs. For instance, Lennon and McCartney invited George and Ringo (and friend, Pete Shotton) to the lyric writing session for “Eleanor Rigby.” Paul had written most of the music for that one, but all of the Beatles contributed to the lyrics. Not only that, but George came up with the words AND the musical hook for the “Ah, look at all the lonely people” section. And Ringo made up many of the memorable lines, including ”writing the words to a sermon that no one will hear” and “wearing a face that she keeps in a jar by the door.” George often contributed musical bits to Lennon/McCartney songs without receiving any credit. For instance, it was George who came up with the guitar riff for “And I Love Her.” The titles of the Beatles songs “A Hard Day’s Night” and “Eight Days a Week” were both based upon things Ringo said to Lennon and McCartney. Lennon and McCartney were the main writers for the Beatles, but they were influenced by their friends and band mates.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who was the primary lead vocalist for most songs on The Beatles albums (excluding the White Album)?
Answer: The Beatles did NOT have a “primary lead vocalist.” The band had four members, each of whom sang lead vocals at times. In my count of the “official” Beatles albums and singles, Ringo sang lead 11 times and George sang lead 28 times. Simply count the songs on which each sang lead vocals. JOHN SANG THE MOST LEAD VOCALS, a half dozen songs more than Paul. Also, there are many songs that you have to say are duets between John and Paul. For example, both sang lead on different sections of “A Day in the Life.” And songs like “Two of Us” are duets all the way. And I didn’t exclude the “White Album.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Is it possible to copyright the name "The Beatles" for a band?
Answer: No. Copyright Law protects original works of artistic expression, including songs and sound recordings. Copyright Law does not apply to band names. The name “The Beatles” is protected by Trademark Law. Trademark Law protects the name, logo and image of businesses providing products of services. The band “The Beatles” broke up in 1970, but their recordings are still sold, streamed and performed and their songs are still printed, recorded and performed. The songs and recordings are protected by Copyright Law. Trademark Law protects the source of those songs and recordings.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What was the reason behind the Beatles releasing short albums?
Answer: The Beatles did not release any “short” albums. They released 12 studio albums, with an average of 14 tracks on each. (The “White Album” was a double album with 30 tracks on it.) The first 7 albums were released on Parlophone Records in the UK and they each had 14 tracks on them. Unfortunately, the Beatles’ North American record company was Capitol Record, which converted those 7 albums into 10 albums for the North American market, with ten songs on each album. The songs were presented in a random fashion with little relationship between the Beatles’ original creations and the Capitol versions. North American fans of the Beatles never heard the way the band wanted classic albums such as “Rubber Soul” and “Revolver” presented until the release of the CDs in the late 1980’s. Needless to say, the Beatles were very unhappy with the way Capitol reconfigured their albums. Fortunately, the Beatles catalog has harmonized worldwide and all 219 songs the Beatles intended for commercial release are there.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Which members of The Beatles have acted in multiple movies?
Answer: All four of the Beatles acted in “A Hard Day’s Night,” “Help!”, “Magical Mystery Tour,” and the closing scene of “Yellow Submarine.” They each appeared as themselves in the documentaries “Let it Be” and “Get Back.” Paul starred in his “Give My Regards to Broad Street” and had a cameo in one of the “Pirates of the Carribean” movies. John famously appeared in “How I Won the War” and several private projects. George produced 23 films for Handmade Films including “Monty Python’s Life of Brian” and “Time Bandits.” Ringo had perhaps the most significant film career, with dozens of appearances in diverse movies such as “Candy,” “The Magic Christian,” “200 Motels,” “Son of Dracula,” “Listzomania”, “The Last Waltz” and “Caveman.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did the Beatles have any hits in America after "Hey Jude"?
Answer: “Hey Jude” was #1 on the Billboard charts in September, 1968. The Beatles had four more #1 hits after “Hey Jude”: “Get Back” (May, 1969), “Something” (October, 1969), “Let it Be” (March, 1970) and “The Long and Winding Road” (May, 1970). They also had several additional hits after “Hey Jude,” including “Revolution” (#12 in September, 1968), “Don’t Let Me Down” (#35 in May, 1969) and “The Ballad of John and Yoko” (#8 in June, 1969).

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can we hear Ringo Starr playing any instruments other than drums/percussion on any Beatles' songs?
Answer: Besides piano on “Don’t Pass Me By” and Hammond organ on “I’m Looking Through You,” Ringo was credited with playing harmonica on “Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite,” comb and paper on “Lovely Rita” and suitcase on “Words of Love.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who sang lead vocals on "She Loves You" by The Beatles?
Answer: This is one of those songs I’d call a vocal duet between John and Paul, with quite a bit of vocal backing from George. John and Paul essentially sang the melody in unison on the choruses. They sang the verses sometimes in unison and other times in harmony with Paul a third higher. I suppose one could argue that Paul sang the melody on those parts. However, I’ve noticed that John’s vocals are always mixed louder than the other two on this song, especially in live versions. Thus, I question the idea that there is even supposed to be a dominant or lead vocal part. Needless to say, the best thing about the vocals is the song’s last chord—a G6 chord on the last “Yeah.” Paul sang the high G, George sang the E above middle C and John sang the D above middle C.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What’s your opinion on the song “In My Life” by the Beatles and do you think it is a song that should be played at a funeral?
Answer: I played and sang “In My Life” at a funeral for a friend of mine less than two weeks ago. That song has a truly beautiful lyric and melody, but I discovered that for a funeral it has a minor problem. In the first verse the singer reminisces about lost friends and remembered places, but in the second verse the singer is clearly singing a love song that is more romantic in nature. My general rule is to NEVER change a songwriter’s words, but I chose to change a single word. I changed the word “love” the first time it’s used in the second verse to “friendship.” That’s very subtle. But it made me feel comfortable that I was singing about the collective loss of our friend and not about romantic love. In retrospect, I’m sure that I over-thought the entire issue. Needless to say, the song was very well-received and is appropriate for funerals.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can a Beatles song really be a Beatles song if all four Beatles didn't play on it?
Answer: Yes. A Beatles song is any song that the Beatles decided to include on any of the band’s 13 official albums. There were at least 3 songs that NO Beatles played on. No Beatle played on “Eleanor Rigby.” Paul, John and George sang on it. No Beatle played on “She’s Leaving Home” (Paul and John sang) or “Good Night” (Ringo sang). Paul completed at least six Beatles songs all by himself. Isn’t “Yesterday” a Beatles song? It’s just Paul singing and playing guitar on that recording. No other Beatles participated. Ditto for “Blackbird,” “Martha My Dear” and several others. George did some Beatles songs by himself (including “Within You Without You”), as did John (“Julia”). 14 of the 30 tracks on the White Album did not include all four Beatles. Isn’t “Back in the USSR” a Beatles song? That track didn’t include all four of the Beatles. If you have a rule that all four Beatles had to participate in a song, then you’d have to eliminate at least 1/4 of all the songs the Beatles did from 1966 to their final recording.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did all four Beatles sing and play on every song?
Answer: No. There were three Beatles songs that NO Beatles played on: “Eleanor Rigby” (which had 4 violins, 2 violas and 2 cellos), “She’s Leaving Home” (which had 12 strings) and “Good Night” (which had a 26-piece orchestra). Paul McCartney was the only Beatle to play on “Yesterday,” “Mother Nature’s Son,” “Wild Honey Pie,” “Blackbird,” “Her Majesty” and “Martha My Dear.” George Harrison was the only Beatle to play on “Within You Without You” and “The Inner Light.” John Lennon was the only Beatle to play on “Julia.” Starting as early as 1965, there were sometimes different combinations of Beatles playing on different songs. For example, Paul and Ringo were the only Beatles to play on “For No One” and “Don’t Pass Me By.” John and Paul were the only Beatles to play on “The Ballad of John and Yoko.” George and Ringo were the only Beatles to play on “Love To You.” As far as singing goes, of the songs on the Beatles official albums, Ringo sang lead on 11 songs. But he was strictly a soloist. He never sang backing vocals in the Beatles. George sang lead on 28 songs. When three vocal parts were required, George would usually sing the middle part, with John on the lower part and Paul on the higher part. Paul sang lead on 66 songs and John sang lead on 72 songs. John and Paul were considered to be a duet on 24 songs.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did The Beatles ever have an official number 1 hit single/album in America?
Answer: The Beatles currently hold the all-time record with twenty #1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100. Their new single “Now and Then” entered the charts at #7. If it reaches #1, that would give the Beatles twenty-one #1 hits in the US. The band also had several additional #1 hits in the UK. The band’s album simply entitled “#1” contains 27 #1 hits in the US or UK. The Beatles also currently hold the all-time record with nineteen #1 albums in the US. That includes the album “#1.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who played on 'Abbey Road' besides The Beatles?
Answer: Billy Preston played Hammond organ on “Something” and “I Want You (She’s So Heavy).” George Martin played Hammond organ on “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer,” electric harpsichord on “Because” and Lowrey organ on “Sun King.” There were five songs with orchestral instruments arranged by Martin. “Something” had 21 strings. There were 21 strings and 9 brass on both “Carry That Weight” and “Golden Slumbers.” “The End” had 17 strings and 9 brass. “Here Comes the Sun” had 9 strings and 8 woodwinds.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who holds the record for the most number one singles on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in US history? Why don’t all artists with many number one songs have this record?
Answer: The Beatles hold the record for the most #1 singles on the Billboard Hot 100 chart with 20.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who sang lead on "I'll Be Back", which was one of The Beatles' very last songs recorded together?
Answer: “I’ll Be Back” is hardly one of the Beatles last songs. It was recorded in 1964. The song was written primarily by John and John sang lead with Paul and George on vocal harmonies. It was written for the movie “A Hard Day’s Night” but wasn’t used in the movie. The song wasn’t released in America until Capitol Record’s “Beatles ‘65.” John called the song “an early favorite” for good reason. It’s quite lovely, mysterious and it has a very unusual structure. First the song alternates between the keys of A major and A minor throughout. Second, the song lacks a chorus. There are 3 verses and the title line “I’ll be back again” is sung only as the second line of the first verse and in the last line of the coda. Third, the song has TWO bridges. Lennon and McCartney always referred to the bridge as “the middle eight.” Neither bridge here has 8 bars. The first bridge (starting on “I love you so”) has six bars plus a 2/4 bar. The second bridge (starting on “I thought that you would realize”) is nine bars long plus a 2/4 bar. The form is: Intro, Verse 1, Bridge 1, Verse 2, Bridge 2, Verse 3, repeat Bridge 2, Coda, Repeat and Fade. George played a nylon-stringed classical guitar on the song.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Which Beatle had the most successful solo career after leaving the band, and which one had no solo career?
Answer: ALL of the Beatles had successful solo careers after the band broke up. All four had multiple #1 hits and multiple Top Ten hits. Paul McCartney had the most chart success—22 Top Ten hits and 9 #1’s. McCartney has amassed the strongest catalog in the 53 years he’s worked since the Beatles broke up in 1970. Ringo Starr had 8 Top Ten hits and 2 #1’s. He’s toured extensively with his All-Star band and is still very active. George Harrison had 6 Top Ten hits and 3 #1’s in the 31 years that he was alive following the break-up. He had the best-selling solo Beatles recording—”All Things Must Pass.” And he had the last #1 single by a solo Beatle—1988’s “Got My Mind Set on You.” John Lennon had the shortest solo career—just ten years before he was murdered in 1980. In that time he had 8 Top Ten hits and 2 #1’s. At the time of his death he was tied with McCartney with 3 #1 albums after the split. Lennon, arguably, left the biggest legacy. His peace activism and songs such as “Give Peace a Chance” and “Imagine” may be the most IMPACTFUL of any solo Beatle.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How does John Lennon's estate continue to earn royalties from his music catalog?
Answer: John Lennon’s estate (Yoko Ono and Sean Lennon) makes money from Lennon’s catalog the same ways songwriters have always made money from their songs: Song-publishing and recordings. Generally, the song publisher collects royalties and splits the royalties with the songwriter(s) 50/50 or a more favorable percent to the songwriter (or, in this case, his estate). Lennon’s songs as a solo artist were generally written alone. In those cases, Lennon receives the entire writer’s share. The Beatles songs Lennon wrote were all legally co-credited to Paul McCartney. The two split the songwriters share on every song 50/50. Even songs that McCartney wrote, such as “Yesterday,” are legally split 50/50 with Lennon (and vice-versa). Thus, each writer gets a minimum of 25 cents of each dollar that comes to the publisher. Songwriters (or their estates) make song-writing royalties in the following ways. This is not a complete list: Lennon also still makes record royalties for every Beatles recording that sells. This is a percentage of the retail price and applies to physical copies, digital downloads and albums that are streamed.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How many top 10 albums does Frank Sinatra have on the Billboard 200 after The Rolling Stones?
Answer: Frank Sinatra had 35 albums that charted in the Top Ten on the Billboard 200 in the U.S. Additionally, he had 5 other Top Ten albums in the U.K., for a total of 40. The Rolling Stones had 39 albums that charted in the Top Ten in the U.K. Additionally they had 13 other Top Ten albums in the U.S., for a total of 52. The Stones’ first Top Ten album was in 1964. Sinatra had 17 Top Ten albums post-1964.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How many number one hits does Barry Manilow have?
Answer: Barry Manilow had three songs that went to #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 between 1974 and 1976: “Mandy,” “I Write the Songs” and “Looks Like We Made It.” Manilow didn’t write any of them. In addition, Manilow had ten other songs that achieved #1 on the Adult Contemporary charts between 1974 and 1983. He co-wrote three of those.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who sang lead in "Two Of Us", by The Beatles?
Answer: I would say that there was no lead vocal in “Two of Us.” The two parts, the higher part sung by Paul and the lower part sung by John, were of equal importance. From their very beginning, Paul and John were influenced by the close vocal harmonies of the Everly Brothers, and they were essentially doing Everly Brothers-style harmonies in “Two of Us,” including the Everly Brothers’ use of diatonic thirds. One of the most significant things about the Beatles is that THEY DID NOT HAVE A LEAD SINGER. They had four members, all of whom took turns being the lead singer. On their official albums, John sang lead on 72 songs. Paul sang lead on 66 songs. George sang lead on 28 songs and Ringo sang lead on 11 songs. And there were about 20 songs, like “Two of Us,” that are generally considered to be DUETS between John and Paul. John and Paul’s use of close vocal harmony is what makes the song. This includes the early songs “Love Me Do” and “Please Please Me,” songs such as “If I Fell” and “Day Tripper,” and some of the other songs on the “Let It Be” album, including “I’ve Got a Feeling” and “One After 909.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How did The Beatles record "Let It Be" in one take?
Answer: They didn’t. The Beatles did TWENTY-SEVEN TAKES of “Let it Be” between January 25 and January 31, 1969. George overdubbed a guitar solo on April 30, 1969. On January 4, 1970, George added a second guitar solo, Ringo added some drums and George Martin did brass and cello overdubs. George (Harrison) and Paul and Linda McCartney did vocal overdubs, making a total of 30 takes. The single was released on March 6, 1970.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Do you agree with the lyrics of the song "Imagine", by John Lennon?
Answer: The song is entitled “Imagine” and it asks the listener to imagine no countries, nothing to kill or die for and no more greed or hunger. It asks the listener to imagine people living in peace, living for today and living in brotherhood. In that sense, there’s little in the lyrics to agree or disagree with. I suppose it’s obvious that the singer believes in peace, unity, brotherhood and sharing. And that the singer is opposed to greed, hunger and war. If that’s the message, can anyone disagree with it? Yes, the singer says “imagine no religion.” However, he doesn’t denigrate religion. In fact, Lennon had a religious-like faith in the possibilities of humanity and he described himself as “a religious man.” And the song encourages listeners to think about war and hunger in a respectful and calm way. The only action statement the singer even makes is: ”I hope someday you’ll join us and the world will live as one.” I’d have to say, “Yes. I agree with those lyrics.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who sang the high pitched “la la la la la la la la la la la la”s in Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da by the Beatles? I thought it may have been Yoko at first but I looked and it said she only sang The Continuing Story of Bungalow Bill.
Answer: John and George did the backing vocals on that song. The “la la la la” part was often sung in thirds. When John and George did backing vocals, George would more often than not take a higher part and John the lower.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the Beatles album with the most number one songs on it?
Answer: “1” by the Beatles, which included all 27 #1 hits the band had in the UK or the US. Ha! However, assuming that you want one of the official Beatles albums, the answer is “Help!.” That album included three #1’s: “Ticket to Ride,” “Help!” and “Yesterday.” The three songs were included on the UK version, not on the North American release, which left off “Yesterday.” It’s true that the album “Let it Be” included three #1 songs. However, the single versions of “Get Back” and “Let it Be” that went to #1 were different than the versions that were included on the album. The album was produced by Phil Spector. The singles “Get Back” and “Let It Be” were produced by George Martin.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can we agree that John Lennon was wrong to call some of Paul McCartney's older-sounding songs like Honey Pie "granny songs"? There has to be a better term that fits the beloved song stylings of prior generations Paul grew up hearing before Rock&Roll.
Answer: Well, John was opinionated and not always subtle. He thought that some of Paul’s songs weren’t edgy enough. However, I think John was, in this matter, short-sighted. Today, music that is deliberately composed in an old-fashioned idiom is called “Retro.” Several of McCartney’s songs were retro. There was nothing wrong with that. “When I’m Sixty Four” (1967) evoked British Music Hall of about 50 years earlier. Yes, it was old-fashioned, but it was humorous and jaunty. It’s a great track. And the fact is, in 1965, Herman’s Hermits had a big hit with a COVER of an actual British Music Hall song from 1910, “I’m Henery the Eighth, I Am.” In 1968, Paul recorded his song “Honey Pie,” which harkened back to the days of Rudy Valee in the mid 1920’s. Valee was one of the first “crooners”—a male singer who sounded good on the radio, but whose voice wasn’t strong enough to fill a concert hall in the days before microphones and amplification. Thus, in live situations, Valee sang through a megaphone. “Honey Pie” was another charming track and John, in a rare lead guitar role, played a stylish guitar solo. I’ll bet he had fun doing that, so I don’t know what he was complaining about. Furthermore, the New Vaudeville Band had a #1 hit in 1966 with a similar throwback to the 1920’s—“Winchester Cathedral.” So, even though neither of those songs were particularly edgy, that 1920’s retro style was cool at the time. Some of Paul’s other retro songs, such as “Martha My Dear” and “Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da” are also great. They were playful, fun and well-written. It doesn’t matter that they weren’t edgy, they were good songs. And that’s what counts.

Question: What instruments are used in the song "I Am The Walrus" by The Beatles?
Answer: Lennon played the Hohner Pianet, an electric piano. McCartney, Harrison and Starr played their regular instruments—bass, guitar and drums. There were 16 backup singers. George Martin wrote an arrangement for 8 violins, 4 cellos, 3 French Horns and a single clarinet. Lennon’s words for the song are well-known. He wrote the words to confound listeners. What’s not well-known is the fact that Lennon built the song on a looped sequence of all the major chords. There are only major chords and seventh chords. The structure has been referred to as a harmonic Moebius strip. The words are classic. But I’ve always thought that the music was one of the Beatles strongest compositions.

The album went to #2 in the US. There are two albums produced in the 1990’s, “Live at the BBC,” Volumes 1 and 2, which also sold well.

Question: Did the Beatles write She Loves You?
Answer: Yes. It was one of the handful of songs that John and Paul wrote “eyeball to eyeball.” The two began writing the song after the Beatles did a show with Roy Orbison and Gerry and the Pacemakers in June, 1963. They began the song on the tour bus, continued it when they got back to the hotel and completed it the next day at Paul’s house. It was recorded less than a week later. According to Paul, the song was inspired by a Bobby Rydell song. It was Paul’s idea to write the song from the standpoint of a man (the singer) recounting to a friend what he heard the friend’s estranged girlfriend say to him. John said that he would normally have written it from a first-person standpoint. The musical hook was “She loves you, yeah yeah yeah.” The Beatles began the song with the musical hook, which was the last part of the chorus. Then they did the verse. That was unusual. There was no bridge. That was also unusual. Lennon said that the phrase “yeah yeah yeah” was inspired by listening to Elvis. Lennon also said that the use of falsetto “oooohs” throughout was inspired by the Isley Brothers. George Harrison came up with the G6 chord that the song ends on. George Martin didn’t like it. He found it “corny” because it harkened back to the big band era. However, thankfully, the Beatles won out over Martin and kept the G6 chord. They sang the G6 chord at the end with John on the D, George on the E and Paul on the high G.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Should Lara Trump be in legal trouble for covering the Tom Petty song, "I Won't Back Down"?
Answer: There’s no reason she should be in trouble as long as she follows the provisions of Section 115 of the US Copyright Act. Anyone in the U.S. can record a cover of a song that has been previously distributed to the public. You don’t need anyone’s permission—not the publisher’s and not the songwriter’s. It’s called a “compulsory license” in section 115 because those people cannot deny you permission. The only thing Lara Trump has to do is give notice to the publishers of Petty’s song and pay them 9.1 cents per copy sold. That figure—9.1 cents— is the statutory mechanical royalty rate. The only restrictions that are on the person who records the cover is that “the arrangement shall not change the basic melody or fundamental character of the work.” You also cannot change the words without permission. “I Won’t Back Down” was a co-write between Tom Petty and Jeff Lynne. Petty’s publisher is Gone Gator Music. I don’t know who administers them. Lynne’s music is administered by Sony Music Publishing. They’re not hard to find—they’re the biggest music publisher in the world.

Cramer was a Nashville session player who played on countless country classics such as Patsy Cline’s rendition of “Crazy.” Cramer became a popular performer himself and had a #2 pop hit in 1960 with “Last Date.” Country piano began with Western Swing, a style that originated in Texas in the 1920’s. Country swing bands were the first to add drums, electric instruments and pianos to country music. All Stricklin (1908–1986) was the pianist for Bob Wills and his Texas Playboys from 1933–1942. Moon Mullican (1909–1967) was an important pianist who influenced Jerry Lee Lewis and Rockabilly, a close relative to country. Floyd Domino played with the great Western Swing band Asleep at the Wheel. Harold “Pig” Robbins (1938–2022) was a great session player who played on Charlie Rich’s “Behind Closed Doors” and countless other hits. Ray Charles (1930–2004) helped develop soul music, but Charles also recorded country music. Dave Haywood (born 1982) is the pianist with the band Lady A. Little David Wilkins (born 1945), John Barlow Jarvis (born 1954), Mickey Gilley (1936–2022), Rick Trevino (born 1971), Charlie Rich (1932–1995) and Bobby Ogdin (born 1945) all played piano on their own or other’s hits.

Question: How many musicians have played with The Beatles?
Answer: The band changed their name to “The Beatles” in August, 1960, just before they left for their first Hamburg residency. That’s where I begin my count. At that time, there was John, Paul, George, Stu Sutcliffe and Pete Best. They recorded with singer/guitarist Tony Sheridan in June, 1961. “My Bonnie” was billed as “Tony Sheridan & the Beat Brothers.” Sutcliffe left in early 1962. In August, 1962, the Beatles replaced Best with Ringo Starr. Around this time, drummer Andy White played a couple of sessions with the band. Drummer Jimmie Nichol subbed for Ringo for 8 concerts in the 1964 tour. One non-Beatle guitarist—Eric Clapton— played on one song—”While My Guitar Gently Weeps.” The keyboard players included all four of the Beatles, George Martin, and three others—Billy Preston played organ or electric piano on 13 songs. Nicky Hopkins played a hell of an electric piano solo on the fast version of “Revolution.” And Chris Thomas, recording producer, played on several songs on The White Album. The Beatles occasionally jammed with friends—Klaus Voormann and Donovan come to mind. There were many guest backup singers—Jane Asher, Linda McCartney, Pattie Boyd, Yoko Ono, Eric Clapton, Donovan, Marianne Faithful, Mick Jagger, Brian Jones, Keith Moon, Graham Nash, Keith Richards and Maureen Starkey. (Some of these people may count as “musicians” and some don’t.) There were a number of Indian musicians who were hired by Harrison for “Within You Without You” and “The Inner Light.” One of them was uncredited. Then, there are the dozens of professional orchestral musicians that the Beatles hired for recording sessions. Some of their names are not known. For instance, the orchestral musicians that Phil Spector hired for the “Let It Be” sessions were uncredited. In all, there are right around 200 additional musicians that the Beatles hired. Thus, the total number of musicians the Beatles performed with or recorded with is around 250.

Question: What is the story behind "Can't Do That"? It seems like a forgotten hit, and it's one of the Beatles' strongest melodies from their early years.
Answer: I agree that “You Can’t Do That” is a strong melody and a really good song. It’s probably overlooked because the Beatles simply had so many other great songs at that time. In a span of two weeks between March 14th and March 28th, 1964, six Beatles songs debuted on the American charts. “Twist and Shout” reached #2, “Roll Over Beethoven” reached #68, “Can’t Buy Me Love” #1, “All My Lovin’” #45, “Do You Want To Know a Secret” #2 and “You Can’t Do That” #48. The Beatles were competing with themselves. “You Can’t Do That” was written entirely by John Lennon and credited to Lennon/McCartney. It was the B-side of “Can’t Buy Me Love,” debuting on March 28, 1964. It was included on the album “A Hard Day’s Night.” A performance of the song was filmed for the movie, but it was later cut. Lennon was influenced by hard-edged American R&B. He sings the note F natural on the words “I told you before,” turning the D7 chord played on those words into a D7#9 chord, a dissonant, distinctive and bluesy sound. Lennon played the guitar solo on his Rickenbacker 325. The solo has great energy and is a combination of riffing and playing rhythm guitar-style chords. The song has a prominent cowbell part, played by Paul McCartney. George Harrison made up the great two bar riff that starts the song on solo guitar. Harrison played it on his Rickenbacker 360 12-string. After this song, the two-bar guitar riff beginning became a standard way to start a rocking song. The Rolling Stone’s “Satisfaction” and Paul Revere and the Raiders’ “Kicks” were influenced by this style. Lennon’s lyrics are semi-autobiographical and indicate the jealousy and possessiveness he felt at that time. The same theme is evident in other songs he wrote, including “Run for Your Life” and “Jealous Guy.” In this song, he forbids his girl to so much as “talk to” another guy. The background vocals by Harrison and McCartney are strong. The bridge that begins, “Everybody’s green” is very clever. The single “Can’t Buy Me Love” went to #1 for 5 weeks. The B-side, “You Can’t Do That,” peaked at #48. “You Can’t Do That” is a strong tune that hasn’t attained the status of other Beatles hits. I think the reason is that it just got lost in the shuffle of all the other great songs by the Beatles at the time.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did the Beatles use a lot of piano in their songs?
Answer: No. Not initially. On their first album there was just one song that had piano on it. However, as time went by the Beatles began to have piano on more and more recordings. During the last third of their career, they used piano on more than half the songs. On their first album, “Please Please Me,” there was piano on one song, “Misery.” The piano was played by Beatles producer, George Martin. On the Beatles second album, “With the Beatles,” there was piano on four songs. George Martin played piano on “Not a Second Time,” “You Really Got a Hold on Me” and “Money (That’s What I Want).” Paul McCartney played piano on “Little Child.” On the album “A Hard Day’s Night” there was piano on three tracks, George Martin played piano on “Tell Me Why” and the title track. McCartney played piano on “When I Get Home.” George Martin continued to sometimes play piano on recordings, all the way through “The White Album.” But McCartney eventually became the Beatles main pianist. John Lennon also played piano on just about every album. Billy Preston played electric piano and organ with the band in 1969, He played electric piano on 6 tracks on the “Let It Be” album. McCartney played piano on 5 tracks, so there was piano on 11 of 14 tracks. On the last album the Beatles recorded, “Abbey Road,” 9 of the 17 songs had piano. That’s more than 50%. So, during their career the Beatles went from a two-guitar band with “Please Please Me” (an album that had piano on one track) to a band that had piano on most of the songs.

Question: Who wrote 'Blackbird' for The Beatles? What did it mean to him/her, and what was its message to humanity at large?

McCartney has said various things about the origin and meaning of the song. First, he’s said that the lyrics were inspired by a blackbird’s call that he heard while studying with the Maharishi in Rishikesh, India. Secondly, McCartney has also said that the lyrics were inspired by racial tension in the American south. Whichever story you accept, “Blackbird” is one of the best tunes McCartney ever wrote.

Question: What did George Martin and the other 3 Beatles really think about George's 'Within You Without You' on Sgt. Pepper?
Answer: John Lennon said that “Within You Without You” was “one of George’s best songs. One of my favorites of his, too. He’s clear on that song. His mind and his music is clear.” Ringo said, “Within You Without You is brilliant. I love it.” Paul followed the recording sessions, which were led by George Harrison with a group of Indian musicians. Paul even bought a sitar himself. George Martin wasn’t crazy about the song, but later on he said that “it was a very interesting song.” The song is about how the answers to question in life are already within you, so you don’t have to look outside to find the answers. I first heard the song as an 11-year-old in June, 1967. I was struck by the meter changes, the Mixolydian mode, the Indian instruments and the song’s references to “the people who hide themselves behind a wall of illusion.” And then there was Harrison’s addition of a laugh track at the end, which was devastating, given the seriousness of the song. I personally believe, some 56 years later, that the most revolutionary song on “Sgt. Pepper’s” wasn’t “A Day in the Life,” but was “Within You Without You.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the most covered pop song in history, and why do musicians keep covering it?
Answer: According to Guinness World Records, the most covered song in history is “Summertime” by George Gershwin, DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin. Guinness used to list “Yesterday” by Lennon and McCartney in this position. “Yesterday” has been recorded something like 4,000 times. However, “Summertime” has been recorded 67,591 times and counting. “Summertime” is an aria from the 1935 opera “Porgy and Bess.” The music is by George Gershwin and the lyrics are by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin (George’s older brother). The song has always been popular in its original form as an aria. After its release in 1935, it became popular as a jazz standard. Today it’s considered one of the most important jazz standards and it’s also popular among blues singers and instrumentalists. George Gershwin intentionally tried to create a song that had a resemblance in tone to African American spirituals. “Summertime” has a definite resemblance to “Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child.” The melody is entirely pentatonic, except for the note on the word “high.” Musicians still record the song because it’s such a great melody and lyric and the song is so flexible—it can be done at a fast tempo or slowly, bluesy or classically. It works many ways. I’ve played it so often with so many singers, that I realized one day that it’s the only song that I’ve actually played in every key. It’s been recorded by Billie Holiday, Bill Evans, Louis Armstrong, Janis Joplin, Joni Mitchell, Willie Nelson, Audra McDonald, Lana Del Rey and 67,000 other singers or instrumentalists.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why was "Let It Be" not performed live during concerts of The Beatles but other songs like "Hey Jude" were performed live frequently during their concerts?
Answer: I don’t believe that the Beatles ever performed “Hey Jude” live in concert. The Beatles last official concert was at Candlestick Park in San Francisco on August 29, 1966, two years before “Hey Jude” was released. The Beatles impromptu rooftop concert took place on Jan. 30, 1969. They didn’t perform “Hey Jude.” And the promo video of them performing “Hey Jude,” with David Frost as host, was not recorded live—it was largely mimed. They filmed that promo video at Twickenham Film Studios on September 4, 1968. They filmed three takes and edited parts of two takes into the final cut, using the first half of the first take and the second half of the third take. The crowd of 300 fans who spill onstage and sing with the Beatles were extras, recruited specifically for the shoot. Because of Musicians Union rules, the Beatles were forced to hire 36 orchestral musicians. However, the musicians’ performance that day was not recorded. The Beatles performed the song to a pre-recorded track. The Beatles all appear to be singing and playing, but what’s heard in the final video, except for some of McCartney’s vocals, is the pre-recorded track, not their performance that day. The piano heard in the video is the hundred-year-old Bechstein grand piano that McCartney played in the recording studio, not the little upright seen in the video. According to Mark Lewisohn, Paul McCartney sang along with his own pre-recorded vocal in the body of the song and then sang live in the long ad-libbed final refrain.

Question: What is the name of the Motown song that the Beatles recorded?

It was recorded by Barrett Strong in 1959 and was the very first hit record for Motown. “Please Mr. Postman” was written by Georgia Dobbins, William Garrett, Freddie Gorman, Brian Holland and Robert Bateman. Question: When a distributor says I need documents that proves that I own a song or received rights to distribute a song, what should the document say?

You, as song owner, have to give the distributor some sort of assurance that you can give him the right to distribute the Song. The words “represents” and “warrants” are the words the distributor wants to hear.

Question: Do any Beatles songs have a lot of chord changes?
Answer: Yes. The Beatles wrote some songs that had a lot of chord changes. I think their record was “You Never Give Me Your Money.” That song, written primarily by Paul McCartney, has, if I’ve counted correctly, 28 different chords in it. 28 chords is far more chords than one would normally find in a popular song that lasts a little over four minutes. The chief reason is that the song is made up of six different sections. There are usually only two or three sections in a popular song. The first four sections are in the key of C and the last two are in the key of A. Each section introduces more chords. The first section (“you never give me your money”) contains seven chords done in a circle of fifths, starting on A minor. The next section (“out of college…”) introduces several new chords. Section three (”oh, that magic feeling”) goes into a B flat tonality. Section 4, the guitar solo, is back to C but introduces about eight new chords, in a quick surge of harmonic color. Section five (“one sweet dream”) is in the key of A and introduces several new chords. The song ends on another section (“one two three four…”) that is a repeat and fade. It’s a very harmonically rich song-–28 chords in all. McCartney’s “Martha My Dear” also has a lot of chord changes—it has 20 chords in it. There are 8 chords in the piano solo intro alone, which is also the verse. Another section (“hold your head up”) introduces some more chords, as does the third section (“take a good look around you”). George Harrison’s “Something” is also a harmonically dense song. It contains 18 chords. “Something” begins in the key of C, but the bridge goes into A major. The Beatles did write some songs that have lots of chord changes. The Beatles also wrote songs with very few chord changes. “Tomorrow Never Knows” has a total of two chords—C and Bb/C.

Question: How many concerts did The Beatles perform live? How many of them were official recordings released for public consumption (including some from live albums)?
Answer: The Beatles performed nearly a thousand live concerts, from August 1960 to their last live performance on Jan. 30, 1969, when they played on the rooftop of their Apple Corp headquarters in London. They worked very hard in 1961, when they played about 200 times in the UK and about 90 times in Hamburg, Germany. In 1962, they played fewer times in Hamburg but more times in the UK. In 1963, they constantly played in the UK and managed a short tour in Sweden. They began playing in the US after their Ed Sullivan Show appearance in February, 1964. That year they also managed to tour France and Australia/New Zealand. Every year from 1961 to 1966, the number of gigs they played declined. They gave up concertizing after their performance at Candlestick Park in San Francisco on Aug 29, 1966. There are perhaps 200 Beatles recordings. But the ONLY official Beatles recordings are their 12 original UK studio albums, the US “Magical Mystery Tour” album and the “Past Masters Volumes One and Two” album which contains all the studio recordings not on the other albums. Their US Capitol Records albums were repackaged from their British releases. The British albums contained 14 songs per album. Capitol put 10 songs on each album. Capitol put the songs in a different order, renamed the albums, used different cover art, and added reverb for no reason. Only with the album “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band” did Capitol match what the Beatles, their manager and their producer wanted their albums to actually look like and sound like. The Beatles NEVER released a live album when they were a band. The first live Beatles recordings were released in 1977 (7 years after the Beatles broke up). The “Live at the Star Club in Hamburg, Germany” album used very low fi recordings. So did “The Beatles at the Hollywood Bowl.” There are a few decent live recordings on some compilations such as the three “Anthology” albums. However, the Beatles may be the only major band of the 1960’s that didn’t release a single live album when they were a band.

Question: What is the story behind the song "Try to Remember" from "The Fantasticks"?

Tom Jones (the lyricist and not the singer) passed away at age 95 on August 11, 2023. The Fantasticks is based on an 1894 play by Edmond Rostand. The original off-Broadway production ran for 42 years (1960–2002) and 17,162 performances, making it the longest running musical in history. An off-Broadway revival ran another 4,390 performances between 2006 and 2017. The song “Try to Remember” is the musical’s best-known song and has been recorded by numerous artists. The song is about nostalgia. It was sung in the original production by actor Jerry Orbach, who played a mysterious bandit named El Gallo. Harvey Schmidt said that he wrote the music in a single sitting. The tune is a tender waltz with a repetitive, easily remembered melody and universal appeal. It’s in a simple A-A-A form. The lyrics, by Jones, begin with the title, which is repeated four times in both the first and second verses. There are three verses in A-A-A form. The first verse uses rhymes of the words “mellow,” “yellow” and “fellow” and use other similar-sounding words such as “callow” and “follow.” The words in the second verse use similar rhymes, such as “willow” and “billow.” All three verses end with the word “follow,” which is then repeated another 8 to 9 times in an echo fashion. The Fantasticks, with its small cast and minimal production requirements, is one of the most widely produced musicals in the world.

Question: Just how humiliated was George Harrison when "MY SWEET LORD" was a tremendous hit, received thousands of accolades and awards, got extreme praise from his friends, only to be discovered that he stole the song?
Answer: George Harrison wasn’t humiliated. And he didn’t steal the song. He was found liable for copying two melodic phrases—one was three notes long and the other was five notes long. The judge said that Harrison did it “subconsciously.” But Harrison was not humiliated. In fact, in November, 1976, right on the heels of the trial, Harrison released a single entitled “This Song” that reached #25 on the American charts. “This Song” was a brilliant and funny commentary on his recent legal travails. It made fun of the judge in the “He’s So Fine” case, parodied the plaintiffs’ legal strategy, and questioned the idea that the repetition of THREE notes can constitute copyright infringement. Harrison never deviated from his story, which was that when he picked up his guitar and started singing the word “Hallelujah” over a two-chord progression, he had been inspired by the Edwin Hawkins Singers version of “O Happy Day” (a spiritual that is Public Domain and no longer in copyright), not by any other song. Anyone can hear the similarities in tone between “O Happy Day” and Harrison’s “My Sweet Lord.” I suppose that anyone can also hear similarities between Harrison’s “My Sweet Lord” and the song “He’s So Fine.” Harrison became conscious of the similarity between his tune and “He’s So Fine” only after he was sued. “Why didn’t I realize?” he later said. “It would have been easy to change a note here or there.” As it was, Harrison was found liable for subconscious copyright infringement for the similarity in two melodic phrases—one a three-note phrase and the other a five-note phrase. “My Sweet Lord” had so much going for it—the unusual use of Hindu mantras, Phil Spector’s Wall of Sound (where it really worked), the first use of Harrison’s signature slide guitar technique, and the band on the recording that included Eric Clapton, Pete Ham, Peter Frampton, Gary Booker, Bobby Whitlock, Klaus Voorman, Ringo Starr and Alan White. Harrison eventually ended up owning both songs —”My Sweet Lord” and “He’s So Fine,” which he bought for $587,000. Harrison always played “My Sweet Lord” in all his concerts. Harrison even recorded a couple of new versions before he died. The song is still a popular cover tune. George Harrison may have been frustrated or disappointed by the legal history of “My Sweet Lord.” But he was never humiliated.

He wrote the arrangements for nearly all the really important Beatles songs. He wrote the string quartet arrangement for “Yesterday” and deliberately incorporated Paul’s help. He played the “harpsichord” solo on “In My Life” (which was really a piano solo). He performed the miracle edit on “Strawberry Fields Forever,” melding two takes in different tempos and different keys into one. He played keyboards on more than 30 Beatles songs (three times the number that Billy Preston played on). He played piano, organ, harmonium and harpsichord. He helped develop all the Beatles’ songwriting abilities and recording chops by finding ways to make the Beatles’ creative ideas work in practical terms in the studio. Martin was never a part of The Fab Four because he was of an older generation—he was 14 years older than John Lennon. Martin dressed and wore his hair conservatively. He didn’t write any songs on Beatles albums (except for some incidental music from the soundtrack of “Yellow Submarine”). Martin didn’t perform on stage. Martin wasn’t a rock star. He was a producer, arranger and musician. And, he was, in my opinion, the Fifth Beatle.

Question: Did The Beatles allow many of their early hits to be released as singles in America before they became huge there (like "Please Please Me", "She Loves You", etc.)?
Answer: No. Capitol Records had the North American rights to the Beatles from the beginning. But Capitol resisted putting out any Beatles recordings because Capitol was an old-fashioned and myopic company. The Beatles had to scramble to get any distribution of their early singles in the U.S. Fortunately, they were able to line-up distribution for early singles through Tollie Records, VeeJay Records and Swan Records. Capitol didn’t put out any Beatles product until just before the group’s imminent appearance on Ed Sullivan in February, 1964. Capitol was, overall, a terrible record company for the Beatles, but the Beatles succeeded in spite of them. The Beatles official EMI Recordings always had 14 songs on them. But Capitol nickel and dimed the listening public by putting just 10 songs on each album. Therefore, they took the EMI records that had been carefully sequenced for maximum musical impact and reconfigured them. Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How much money did the Beatles make in royalties from other bands covering their songs?
Answer: The Beatles are not who make royalties from other artists covering songs they recorded. The songwriters in the Beatles are the ones who make the money. First, let me explain a little about cover recordings. Anyone can cover a Beatles song. You don’t need anyone’s permission. Section 115 of the U.S. Copyright Act states that once a nondramatic musical work has been recorded and distributed to the public, “any other person” has the right to record and distribute “phonorecords” (i.e. recordings) of the song, as long as they comply with certain provisions of the act. There are two provisions to comply with. The person making the cover recording must serve notice on the copyright holder. In the case of Lennon/McCartney songs, the copyright holder is Sony/ATV Music Publishing. Then, the person must pay the statutory “mechanical royalty” for every copy that is made and distributed. The statutory mechanical royalty is 9.1 cents. It’ll cost the person recording the cover song 9.1 cents for every copy made and distributed. Now, how much money do Lennon and McCartney make from others covering their songs? The answer is: a significant amount of money but probably a lot less than you think. Take some actual covers of Beatles songs and figure it out. For example, the jazz pianist Brad Meldau has recorded a recent solo piano album entitled “Your Mother Should Know - Brad Meldau Plays the Beatles.“ The album has ten Beatles songs on it (all written by Lennon and McCartney). Meldau is a great jazz pianist, but I’d say a high estimate of the total sales of that recording would be maybe 100,000 copies. Ten songs times 100,000 copies times the statutory royalty of 9.1 cents equals $91,000. Meldau should have paid Sony/ATV $91,000 in mechanical royalties for the right to record 10 Beatles songs on an album that sold 100,000 copies. Sony/ATV receives the royalty payment. They keep 50%, which is the standard publishing deal—50% to the songwriter(s), 50% to the publisher. They pay the other 1/2 to Lennon and McCartney. That means they split $45,500 between Lennon and McCartney. They send $22,750 to Paul McCartney and $22,750 to Yoko Ono, who receives Lennons’ royalties. The song “Yesterday” is said to have the most cover versions of any Beatles song. I’ve heard that there are 3,000 cover versions. In some instances these cover versions were by name artists. For example, Ray Charles recorded “Yesterday.” But in most cases the cover versions are by small timers. Let’s say that the average cover version of “Yesterday” sold 10,000 copies. (That’s actually significantly higher than I think is the real figure.) 10,000 copies times 3,000 versions times 9.1 cents is $2,730,000. $2.7 million in royalties for those thousands of cover versions. Sony/ATV receives the mechanical royalty checks adding up to $2,730,000 and they keep 50% and divide the other 50% between Lennon and McCartney. Wait a minute, didn’t Paul write “Yesterday” in its entirety and wasn’t he the only Beatle to play on the recording? Well, Yes and Yes. But the song is credited to Lennon and McCartney. Lennon and McCartney divide the royalties equally for “Yesterday,” as well as for their other co-written songs. So Sony/ATV takes $1,365,000 and divides it equally, sending $682,500 to McCartney and $682,500 to Yoko. That represents the entire songwriter royalty for the 3,000 cover versions of “Yesterday” recorded since 1965. $682,500 is a nice chunk of change. But wouldn’t you expect that the royalty for those 3,000 cover versions of “Yesterday” would be more? That’s what I mean when I say that the money is less than you might think.

Question: Which Beatle wrote most of the songs for The Beatles? How many songs did each Beatle write for the band?

Answer: Freddie Mercury sang primarily in his middle range on “Bohemian Rhapsody.” He neither sang at his highest range nor at his lowest on that song. Question: What was the highest singing voice of the Beatles? Who would have been their successor as frontman if they were still alive today? Why that person specifically?
Answer: Paul McCartney usually sang the highest part. That wasn’t necessarily the lead voice. George Harrison took the middle part when there were three parts. Question: Did the Beatles ever record two different versions of the same song, one for an album and one for single release?
Answer: There are two versions of “Revolution” and three versions of “Let It Be.” “Revolution 1” is the version on the White Album. It was recorded on May 30, 1968. It’s in the key of A and is played at a very relaxed tempo. It has definite bluesy elements. Its backing vocals repeat “shoo-be-do-wop” and it has a horn track. “Revolution” was recorded about 6 weeks later, on July 9–13, 1968. It’s in the key of B-flat and is at a very fast, rocking tempo with a screaming John Lennon vocal. It’s got a stellar electric piano part played by Nicky Hopkins that is possibly the most smokin’ keyboard part that exists on any Beatles record. “Revolution” was released in August, 1968 as a single. The Beatles recorded three versions of “Let It Be.” “Let It Be” was first released as a single. It was recorded in January, 1969, but wasn’t released as a single until March 6, 1970, 15 months later. The single was produced by George Martin. It’s 3:50 in length. It’s beautifully mixed. It uses the same basic tracks as the album version, but Paul’s vocal, piano and electric piano all sound cleaner and more full. The “Let It Be” album version was produced by Phil Spector. It clocks in at 4:02. It has a re-recorded Harrison guitar solo that is a bit more rocking than the single. There is a very prominent digital delay on Starr’s hi-hat. The orchestration is heavier. Finally, there is “Let it Be Naked.” That track used a different piano track played by Paul than the first two. Thus, the little piano glitch at 2:58 in the piano, which was in the first two, is not to be heard in the “Naked” version. Billy Preston played a nice organ part on all the versions of “Let It Be.” Preston’s organ is almost always identified as a Hammond B-3 organ. But I believe that Preston more likely played a Lowrey Heritage organ.

Question: What are your thoughts on The Beatles' melodies in pop or rock music?
Answer: Primary Beatles songwriters John Lennon and Paul McCartney created dozens of tuneful, memorable and well-constructed melodies. (So did Beatle George Harrison, but I’ll only be looking at Lennon/McCartney songs.) I think that the strength of their melodies is a major reason, perhaps the biggest reason, that Beatles music has remained so popular for more than 50 years after the band broke up. I grew up with the Beatles. I was eight years old in 1964 when the Beatles first appeared on Ed Sullivan and 15 in 1970 when they broke up. People my age can generally sing or hum or whistle some Beatles melodies. So can millions of fans who’ve become familiar with their music in the last 50 years. Melody is clearly the most important musical element of a pop song. It’s the tune that we hum or whistle unaccompanied when we walk down the street or take a shower. Popular songs are often perceived as being the equivalent of their melodies, sometimes to the exclusion of other musical elements, such as the tempo, the beat, the instrumentation, the harmonies and even the words of the songs. A melody is defined as “a linear succession of musical tones that a listener perceives as a single entity.” Consider how the memory works when it comes to melody. Let’s use, as an example, the melody of the Beatles song “Hey Jude,” principally written by Paul McCartney. The key in which McCartney sang the song (F major) is irrelevant. So is the chordal accompaniment (which was basic triads, minor 7th chords and 7th chords). The remembered melody has nothing to do with the actual pitch on the record. The memory stores the relationships in the melody, that is, the intervals between the notes of the melody. Melodies move from one note to the next in three ways: repetition of a single pitch, movement either up or down by step, and movement either up or down by leap of an interval that’s a minor third or greater. The melody of the first phrase of “Hey Jude” (with the lyrics, “Hey Jude, don’t make it bad”) begins with a falling minor third, followed by a rising major third on the same two notes. That’s fallowed by a note that rises one step and then a note that falls an interval of a fifth. What’s important is the relationship between the intervals. That remains the same no matter what key it’s in, or what harmony is used in the accompaniment, or what tempo is chosen, etc. When commentators write about the Beatles, a common statement is that McCartney is the real melodist in the Beatles—the one who wrote the best tunes. Certainly, McCartney wrote many great tunes. He had a real talent for that. However, Lennon was no slouch. He also displayed a great talent for creating melody. Below I’ve listed ten songs that were principally written by John Lennon and ten that were principally by Paul McCartney. These are ten melodies that represent the strengths of each writer. Lennon songs: If I Fell, A Hard Day’s Night, Ticket to Ride, You’ve Got to Hide Your Love Away, Help!, Norwegian Wood, Good Night, Julia, This Boy, and All You Need Is Love. McCartney songs: And I Love Her, Yesterday, Eleanor Rigby, For No One, Here There and Everywhere, She’s Leaving Home, Blackbird, Let It Be, Penny Lane, and Hey Jude. As I said earlier, melodies can repeat a note, move up or down by step or move up or down by a leap of a third or more. It’s often said that a good melody should utilize all three types of movement. But McCartney’s “Yesterday,” a consummate melodic pop song if there ever was one, moves mostly by step. In the A section, played musically 4 times, there are only five instances of notes moving by interval. Four times the melody moves up by an interval of a third and once it moves down by a fourth. Otherwise, all the melodic motion is by step. On the other hand, just the first phrase of McCartney’s “Here There and Everywhere,” contains four leaps upward and two movements do...

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Was Let It Be the last Beatles album?
Answer: I consider “Abbey Road” to be the last Beatles album. “Abbey Road” was recorded between February and August, 1969. It was released in September, 1969. “Let It Be” was recorded by the Beatles, nearly in its entirety, between January and April, 1969, well before “Abbey Road.” The single “Get Back” was released in April, 1969. The album was subsequently abandoned while the Beatles worked on “Abbey Road.” Three of the Beatles returned to the studio for two final days on January 3 and 4, 1970. Paul, Ringo and George were there for the final recording session by the Beatles as a band. John had already left the group. The remaining Beatles recorded George’s “I Me Mine” and did some minor vocal overdubs on “Let It Be.” That was the only work done by the Beatles on the album “Let It Be” after April, 1969. In March, 1970, Beatles manager Allen Klein hired Phil Spector to complete the “Let It Be” project. Spector came to Abbey Road Studios and began mixing the tapes on March 23, 1970. Spector recorded his lavish orchestral and choral overdubs for “The Long and Winding Road,” “I Me Mine” and “Across the Universe” on April 1, 1970. He employed 50 musicians on that day, including Ringo Starr who played drums to keep the 50-musician ensemble together. Spector mixed those songs the next day, thereby completing his production of the album. The “Let It Be” album was released on May 8, 1970. I consider “Abbey Road” to be the final Beatles album because all the Beatles work on “Let It Be,” except for one song and overdubs on one other, was completed long before “Abbey Road” was recorded and more than a year before “Let it Be” was released.

Question: Why did John Lennon only ever play rhythm guitar for The Beatles and occasionally, keyboards too?
Answer: John Lennon played the following instruments on various Beatles records: electric guitar, acoustic guitar, piano, electric piano, organ, harpsichord, harmonium, Mellotron, Moog synthesizer, harmonica, banjo, ukelele, bass guitar, lap steel guitar, drums, various percussion instruments and tenor sax. If you don’t count the percussion instruments, he played 16 different instruments on Beatles records. George Harrison played 14 instruments on Beatles records. Paul McCartney played 13 instruments on Beatles records. Ringo Starr played drums and numerous percussion instruments on Beatles records. He also played organ, piano and harmonica. All the Beatles were multi-instrumentalists and of the Fab Four, Lennon played the most instruments on Beatles records.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did Ringo Starr write the drum parts for The Beatles?
Answer: Ringo created and played the drums parts on nearly every official Beatles recording. An exception was the album version of “Love Me Do.” Ringo’s studio performance was used on the original single release. But George Martin hired studio drummer Andy White to play the drums on the album version. Also, Paul McCartney played the drums on several tracks on the White Album when Ringo “quit” the Beatles for a while. McCartney played on “Dear Prudence,” “The Ballad of John and Yoko” and “Martha My Dear.” McCartney and George Harrison both played drums on the session for “Back in the USSR,” and they co-created a drum part. It’s said that Paul McCartney came up with the drum beat for “Ticket to Ride.” Of course, Ringo played it like no one else could.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who played the piano on "Here Comes The Sun" by the Beatles?
Answer: No one played the piano on “Here Comes the Sun.” There’s no piano on the recording. However, George Harrison played two keyboard instruments on the recording—the Moog synthesizer and the Harmonium. Harrison used the Moog to create several sounds that he doubled the melody with. For example, the Moog doubled the melody in bars 5–8. The Moog was used to create a different sound to double the melody in the seond verse. And the Moog was used to create a nice “buzzy” sound in octaves at “sun sun sun, here it comes.” The studio notes say that Harrison also played a harmonium, which is a pump organ. Lennon famously played one in the recording and video of “We Can Work It Out.” Here, Harrison probably played the harmonium popular in Indian Kirtan music, which is a smaller harmonium usually played with the right hand and pumped with the left hand. The harmonium track isn’t real explicit. Harrison probably used the harmonium to double the sustained chords in the strings.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the worst song on Abbey Road by the Beatles?
Answer: In my opinion, the worst song on “Abbey Road” is “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer.” It’s a Paul McCartney song about a student named Maxwell Edison who murders people by bashing them over the head with a silver hammer. The story is dumb and juvenile. The music is 1920’s music hall schmaltz. The other three Beatles hated it and resented the fact that Paul made them work on it so hard and so long. John simply said, “I hate it.” George explained it by saying, “Paul would make us do these really fruity songs.” Ringo remembered it as “the worst track we ever had to record. It went on for fucking weeks. I thought it was mad.” Beatles biographer Ian MacDonald described it as a “ghastly miscalculation” and a “lapse of taste” in which McCartney, “the immature egotist frittered away the group’s patience and solidarity on sniggering nonsense.” MacDonald said that more than any other recording, “it shows why the Beatles broke up.” John told Paul that no one else in the band liked “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer” and that it would be a good idea if Paul gave songs like that to outside artists. To that, Paul replied, “I recorded it because I liked it.” That basically summed up the reason the Beatles broke up. Paul liked the song, even though no one else in the band did. More importantly, Paul didn’t care about the opinion of the others. Mal Evans was good on the anvil.
