Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Who wrote most of The Beatles' hits? Do you think that happened because John Lennon and Paul McCartney mostly wrote together, while Ringo Starr mostly wrote with John Lennon?
Answer: George Harrison wrote 22 Beatles songs. Ringo Starr wrote 2 Beatles songs on his own and was credited with fractions of two others. Contrary to the assertion in the question, he did not write with John Lennon. George Harrison helped him out, uncredited, on “Octopus’s Garden.” The Beatles recorded 23 cover songs on their “official” albums. Other than those 47 songs, John Lennon and Paul McCartney co-wrote all the Beatles songs, more than 180 of them. The two were the leaders of the band, the most talented songwriters (at least initially) and were older than George Harrison, who they always treated as a kid brother. Lennon and McCartney made an agreement early in their career to credit every Beatles song that either of them wrote, either individually or together, to the songwriting team of Lennon/McCartney. Early in their career they sometimes wrote together “eyeball to eyeball.” Beatles experts agree that 18 Lennon/McCartney songs can be characterized as 50/50 collaborations. More often, one would be the “principal songwriter” of a composition and the other would offer advice and input. Both of them had input on the vast majority of Lennon/McCartney songs, although there were a few songs that were solely written by either Lennon or McCartney without input from the other. Beatles experts usually credit Lennon with being the principal writer of 72 songs and McCartney with 70. Lennon was the principal writer of more “hits,” but McCartney was the principal writer of far more #1 hits, especially in the years 1968–1970.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Would the Beatles have survived if Paul and John had agreed with the White Album to take full credit for their own songs and dropped the Lennon/McCartney credit except for when they did work together on a song?
Answer: Yes, they would have survived. The Lennon-McCartney credit was the most famous in the world and their collaboration proved to be the most successful of all songwriting teams. However, I think most fans had figured out by 1965 or so that one of the two was generally the principal songwriter for each song and that the principal songwriter sang lead on his songs. As far as the actual contribution by the other, it really depended on each song. With the White Album Lennon and McCartney seemed to have general disregard for each other’s songs and they did most of the overdubbing on their own songs. The majority of the songs on the White Album were written by one of them with minimal or even no input from the other. There even were songs on the White Album that were solely recorded by either Lennon or McCartney. Lennon was the only one to perform on the recording of his “Julia.” McCartney was the only one to perform on the recordings of his “Blackbird” and “Wild Honey Pie.” McCartney was the only Beatle to perform on some of his other songs, although the songs had orchestration by George Martin—”Martha My Dear” and “Mother Nature’s Son.” “Birthday” was definitely a 50/50 Lennon/McCartney collaboration. And I believe that Lennon contributed some lyrics to “Rocky Raccoon.” “Helter Skelter” may have had some contributions by Lennon. But “Revolution 9” was a collaboration between Lennon, George Harrison and Yoko Ono. Ono also contributed to “Bungalow Bill.” Lennon, I think, was the sole writer of “Good Night,” sung by Ringo. I wasn’t there, so I don’t know for sure. But I would guess that the other songs credited to Lennon and McCartney on the White Album could have been solely credited to the principal writer and lead vocalist. The Lennon/McCartney songwriting partnership was unlike the typical songwriting partnerships that came before. Those partnerships comprised a composer and a lyricist, such as George and Ira Gershwin, Richard Rodgers with Larry Hart, Richard Rodgers with Oscar Hammerstein, Carole King and Gerry Goffin, etc. Lennon and McCartney both wrote music and lyrics. Early on they’d write “eyeball to eyeball.” But later in their partnership either of them would write most of a song, often with minimal input from the other and sometimes with no input at all from the other. Even their contemporaries often didn’t understand the dynamics of their relationship. In 1965, I saw the American singer Peggy Lee sing “Yesterday” on a TV show. She introduced the song by saying, “This song has lovely lyrics by John Lennon and beautiful music by Paul McCartney.” It was never that simple.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why is “Here Comes The Sun” considered by many to be the best Beatles’ song?
Answer: “Here Comes the Sun“ is a lovely, sweet song by George Harrison. It has nice lyrical images—”that ice is slowly melting” and “smiles returning to their faces.” And I really like the mixed meter in the bridge (3/8 + 3/8 +5/8 + 4/4). It’s become one of the most streamed Beatles songs and is notable for being one of the first recordings to use the Moog synthesizer. It’s cheerful, tuneful and, without a doubt, an outstanding song. But, “the best Beatles song”? I don’t think so. HCTS was NOT musically or lyrically groundbreaking, like “A Day In the Life,” “Tomorrow Never Knows” and “Strawberry Fields.” Nor was it an instant classic like “Yesterday,” “Eleanor Rigby” or “Hey Jude.” In fact, I don’t even think it’s George Harrison’s best Beatles song. “Something” (also from “Abbey Road”) is a love song for all time and is, in my opinion, a better song. And Harrison wrote other Beatles song that a case could be made for—”Taxman,” “While My Guitar Gently Weeps,” “Within You Without You,” etc. I’m always glad when people appreciate Harrison’s songwriting. And his guitar playing—he had an innate melodic sense and he developed a distinctive lead guitar style. He also broadened the scope of pop music by helping bring worldwide attention to Indian music and spirituality. And he wrote great songs. Thank you, George Harrison.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Did Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr keep any of the money from the Beatles song publishing rights for themselves?
Answer: No. Paul McCartney wrote all of his compositions for the Beatles in collaboration with John Lennon. They shared the publishing 50/50 for all the Lennon/McCartney songs. Lennon’s share is controlled by Yoko Ono, who receives all of Lennon’s royalties. Sean Lennon shares in those royalties. Julian Lennon sued Ono in the past to get some sort of payment in lieu of royalties. Lennon is credited with 50% of the songwriting royalties for all the Lennon/McCartney compositions, included “Yesterday,” a song that McCartney wrote without Lennon’s input and recorded without the participation of any of the other Beatles. That’s because Lennon and McCartney decided long before the Beatles became famous to share equally the songwriting credits and the songwriting royalties for every Beatles song either of them wrote in whole or in part. Ringo was the sole writer of two songs for the Beatles. In addition, he was credited with small shares of a few other songs. Together, they add up to less than three songs. George Harrison wrote 22 Beatles songs. His royalties go to his widow Olivia and his son Dhani.

Question: Do you like “Let It Be” by the Beatles? Why do you think it wasn't a success when released, but became so later on?

Question: Why is a piano's middle C not tuned to an exact note?
Answer: I find that question misleading. In general, the one note on a piano that is tuned to an OUTSIDE STANDARD is the A above middle C, A- 440. From that one note, an experienced piano technician can theoretically tune the rest of the notes on a piano by an assessment of the vibration interaction of various intervals. Modern piano tuning uses the equal temperament method, a compromise tuning that makes playing in all keys possible. For those who have finely tuned musical ears, newly tuned pianos using the equal temperament system often sound out of tune. If the piano tuner correctly applied the beats, then middle C should be 261.626 Hz. Some piano technicians today actually use electronic tuners. If one has an electronic tuner, then one could easily start with a note other than A-440. The tuner could have begun with middle C, i.e. 261.626 Hz. Another thing is that A-440 as a standard is changing. In Europe , most orchestras tune to A-442. My own piano technician uses A-442.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the tempo of "Let It Be" by The Beatles? How does it compare to other popular songs?
Answer: The tempo of “Let It Be” is around 72 beats per minute. That is a standard rock ballad tempo. “Imagine” by John Lennon is the same tempo, as is “Hey Jude,” also by the Beatles. Other ballads of that tempo include “Tiny Dancer” (Elton John), “Peaceful Easy Feeling” (Eagles), “Have I Told You Lately” (Van Morrison) and “What a Wonderful World” (Louis Amstrong). “Let It Be” was released in 1970, which happened to be a very fine year for ballads. Several of the other ballads from that year were played slightly faster, including “Fire and Rain” (James Taylor), “Bridge Over Troubled Water” (Simon and Garfunkel) and “Close to You” (The Carpenters). Others were played slightly slower, such as Elton John’s “Your Song.”

Question: Who sings bass on “Penny Lane” by The Beatles?

Question: What are some underrated songs by John Lennon (as a solo artist)?
Answer: A very underrated solo song by John Lennon is “Grow Old with Me.” It was recorded by Lennon as a demo in 1980 while he was in Bermuda. The recording appeared on his posthumous album “Milk and Honey” in 1984. Inspired by a poem by Robert Browning, it’s a lovely ballad that ranks as one of the greatest wedding songs written in the past 50 years. It has a beautiful, sweet melody. The song was considered as a potential reunion single for the Beatles during the Anthology years. However, the original demo recording was deemed to be of insufficient quality to base a Beatles single on it. The song has been covered by many artists, most notably by Mary Chapin Carpenter and by Lennon’s bandmate Ringo Starr.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: This is not an anti-Yoko question; it's simple curiosity. What do you think the John Lennon of 1963 would have thought or said about his future relationship with Yoko Ono, if it were possible to ask him?
Answer: Frankly, I don’t think that the John of 1963 would have been surprised by his future relationship with Yoko Ono. Lennon married Cynthia Powell in August, 1962, and Julian was born in April of 1963. The Beatles achieved some significant success in the UK in 1963. John’s life experience up to then was rather limited. However, all the qualities that made him John Lennon were already in place. John like to act tough—the way he stood on stage with his guitar was aggressive and sexual. Yet, John took great pains to not be seen in public or to be photographed with his spectacles on. John was charming—he famously charmed the Queen Mother and the royal audience in a show in 1963 (“If you’ll just rattle your jewelry”). But John was bored with domestic life. He was artsy, creative and outspoken. Above all, he was a rebel. He wanted to break out of the mainstream. I think that these are the qualities that drew him to Yoko Ono.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why did some people dislike The Beatles when they came out with their new sound in Rubber Soul/Revolver (the psychedelic era)?
Answer: Some people don’t like change. Those people wanted the Beatles to forever remain the cute mop-tops from “The Ed Sullivan Show.” Some people don’t like unique-sounding music. Those people didn’t like the sound of the sitar in “Norwegian Wood,” the harpsichord-like piano solo in “In My Life” or the fuzz bass in “Think for Yourself.” Some people don’t want popular music to have any thought-provoking content. For those people, ”In My Life” was too wistful, “Nowhere Man” was too downbeat and “Michelle” had French words in it (!). Finally, some people are now (and were then) very anti-drug use. Simply the cover photo of “Rubber Soul” said “drugs used here.” I knew that in 1965 when I was only 10 years old.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Is it true that the Beatles used to meditate?
Answer: All four of the Beatles went to Rishikesh, India in February, 1968, to study Transcendental Meditation with the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. Several other celebrities were there, including members of the Beach Boys, Donovan, Mia Farrow and others. Ringo and his wife Maureen stayed for ten days. Paul McCartney and Jane Asher left after 5 weeks. The most dedicated students were John Lennon and George Harrison. They stayed, with their wives, for more than seven weeks. Harrison became a Krishna devotee, chanted and recorded sacred music such as the “Hare Krishna Mantra.” Presumably, he had a regular meditation practice. Lennon was a spiritual seeker all his life and he found useful tools in TM. He, too, recorded music using ancient, sacred mantas, such as “Jai Guru Deva—Om” in “Across the Universe.” McCartney also seemed to be touched by the experience. Upon return to the UK, he wrote “The Fool on the Hill.”

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is your opinion on why 'Hey Bulldog' is considered one of the most underrated Beatle songs ever written and performed? What do you think makes it so special that it receives such praise from fans and critics?
Answer: The reason “Hey Bulldog” was underrated is that it was under-exposed, having been included on the Beatle’s least commercial album, the “Yellow Submarine” soundtrack, released in January, 1969. That album included two songs that had been hit singles—“Yellow Submarine” and “All You Need Is Love.” It had only four new songs—”Only a Northern Song,” “All Together Now,” “It’s All Too Much” and “Hey Bulldog.” Those songs were all under-exposed. The rest of the tracks consisted of incidental music written by George Martin for the film. “Hey Bulldog” was recorded in February, 1968. I can guarantee that, had “Hey Bulldog” been included on “The White Album,” which was released later that year in November, 1968, (before “Yellow Submarine”) it would have been well-known and well-loved. However, as a 13-year-old Beatles fanatic in 1969, I was hardly aware of that song. I didn’t listen to the “Yellow Submarine” soundtrack. Who did? Based on a great piano riff played by Lennon (who was under-rated as a pianist), the song included an inventive bass line by McCartney, great drums by Ringo and nice guitar by George. John borrowed George’s Gibson SG and played the lead guitar solo. The song was a real rocker. Watch the video recorded live in the studio. The Beatles clearly had a great time creating and recording the song in a single 10-hour session. John and Paul had lots of laughs making up dog sounds. The video shows the boys playing with abandon and the sheer joy of making music.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What are some modern jazz songs that have a similar chord progression to "Take Five" by Dave Brubeck?
Answer: I can’t think of any other jazz songs that have a chord progression similar to “Take Five,” which was written by Paul Desmond, the alto sax player in the Dave Brubeck Quartet. “Take Five” is unusual, of course, for the fact that it’s in 5/4 time, a signature that is not used very often. Its harmony is also unusual—it begins with a one-bar, two-chord vamp on the chords Ebm and Bbm7. This two-chord vamp becomes the basis for the eight-bar A section. Two-chord vamps aren’t necessarily all that unusual in jazz. But a song that shifts from a two-chord vamp in the A section to a major harmonic pattern in the B-section is. And that’s what “Take Five” does. The chords in the eight-bar B section follow a circle of fifths pattern: Cbmaj7, Fm7b5, Bbm7, Ebm7, Abm7, Db7, Gbmaj7. And then it goes around again. By the way, these are NOT the chords found in “The Real Book.” “The Real Book,” for whatever reason, is completely wrong on this song. It leaves out half the chords in the B section. The tune then returns to the A section. The form of the tune is A - B - A. All the solos are played over the two-chord vamp that makes up the chordal pattern for the A section. In the original 1959 album recording Desmond solos and then drummer Joe Morello takes a lengthy solo. Neither the bass player nor Dave Brubeck took a solo. The tune then reprises sections A - B- A and vamp out. There aren’t many jazz tunes written in 5/4 time. And there aren’t many that follow a chord pattern such as the one in “Take Five.” It’s an unusual tune all the way around.

Question: Who is the singer with The Beatles on Hey Bulldog?
Answer: The only singers on “Hey Bulldog” are John Lennon, who sang lead and Paul McCartney, who sang harmony. Both had fun making barking sounds. The song was recorded in a single ten-hour session on Feb. 11, 1968. A camera crew was there to shoot a promo film for “Lady Madonna,” but the Beatles decided to record another song, written primarily by Lennon, while they were there together in the studio. The resulting video is one of the last documents of the band playing with abandon and the sheer joy of making music together. The session was produced by George Martin and Geoff Emerick. Because “Hey Bulldog” only appeared on the “Yellow Submarine” soundtrack album, the song was relatively obscure for many years. However, in the past decade or so, it has become regarded as one of the Beatles’ best rockers. Ringo played drums, John played the piano, Paul played a wonderfully busy bass line and George played lead guitar, although George lent John his Gibson SG and John played the lead solo that was used on the recording.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How do musicians compose music that exceeds their ability to play it? Isn't playing how the idea grows to start with?
Answer: A composer doesn’t need to be able to play the music in order to compose it. For example, I don’t know how to play most orchestral instruments, but I’ve written music for orchestra. I just know what instruments are capable of and what they sound like when you stick them together. I like to compose music without using a piano or without relying on any other instrument. The questioner seems to assume that composing begins with playing. I would say that can be true but is not true in the majority of cases. Obviously, if you want to write music that exceeds your ability to play, you cannot write while using an instrument like a piano. You have to write away from the instrument to imagine music that exceeds your ability to play it. Beethoven had a slow, laborious process of composing, painstakingly reworking the sketches in his notebooks. He seemed to get most of his ideas while taking long walks. Popular composers, such as Duke Ellington, were said to often write in the back seats of taxicabs and the like. Ellington didn’t need a piano. He could hear the music in his head and write it out.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why was it so hard for Paul McCartney to write a song like "In My Life" or "Yesterday"?
Answer: Neither song was hard for McCartney to write. In fact, Paul woke up one morning with the melody for “Yesterday” in his head. He crawled out of bed and went to the piano in his bedroom and played it. The tune arrived complete, like it was dropped on him from heaven. He began to worry that he had subconsciously lifted it from someone else. For months he called the tune “Scrambled Eggs.” He played it for anyone who’d listen. Everyone loved it. He played it so often that people began to get sick of it. Finally, when Paul decided that he really did write the tune, the words “Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away” came to him. The rest of the words came easily. John loved the tune but he said that the words never went anywhere. That worked in Paul’s favor. The words are a mere eleven lines and are fairly vague and can apply to all kinds of situations. And no matter what you think of the words, the tune is nearly perfect. As far as “In My Life” goes, there’s no question that John Lennon wrote all the lyrics. At first, it seems like it’s a philosophical song about memories. But, at some point, you realize that it’s a love song about someone he loves now. The song is wistful, but it’s positive and life-affirming. For years Beatles fans assumed that John had also written the music. But Paul came out in the year 1976 and he claimed that he had written the entire tune. Further, he claimed he had written it very quickly—in about 20 minutes, I believe. Neither song was hard for McCartney to write. The tune for “Yesterday” arrived intact and Paul just had to find some words that fit. And according to Paul himself, “In My Life” was a tune he just knocked off.

Question: Do you think 'My Sweet Lord' is George Harrison's best work as a solo artist?
Answer: Yes, I believe it to be Harrison’s greatest work. I also think that it was the best example of Phil Spector’s “Wall of Sound” technique actually working to its maximum effect. From the opening block of acoustic guitars (played by Harrison, Eric Clapton, Peter Frampton, Pete Ham and others) to the end, the wall of sound worked beautifully. It’s only too bad that Spector, who produced all kinds of girl groups in the early 1960’s, failed to point out to Harrison how similar his melody sounded to the hit song by The Chiffon’s “He’s So Fine.” Had Spector, or any of the others in Harrison’s inner circle done that, Harrison could have avoided the famous lawsuit. And he wouldn’t have gone creatively dry for several years following the lawsuit. And there wouldn’t have been this embarrassing taint that sort of held over Harrison for some time in the 1970’s and ‘80’s.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why did George Martin quit The Beatles after Let It Be but before Abbey Road?
Answer: George Martin never quit on the Beatles. And I think you’ve got the timeline mixed up. Martin was there in January, 1969, for the beginning of the album that eventually became known as “Let it Be.” The album was essentially finished by March, 1969, but it was placed on the back burner by the Beatles themselves. Meanwhile, during 1969, George Martin was there to supervise the recording and produce the “Abbey Road” album. That recording project began in February, 1969 and the “Abbey Road” album was released on Sept. 26, 1969. Not only did Martin produce the album, but he played the electric harpsichord on “Because.” After “Abbey Road“ was released, the “Let It Be” album was picked up again. Martin supervised the last Beatles recording session in January, 1970, which was dedicated to recording Harrison’s’ “I Me Mine.” The tapes for “Let It Be” were sent by Beatles manager Allen B. Klein to Phil Spector to complete in March and April of 1970.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: How did the Beatles manage writing songs without knowing how to read or write musical notes? Did they use tablature, for example, when composing songs like "Yesterday"?
Answer: Music is an aural art and it’s not necessary to know how to read music notation in order to play music, sing music or create new music. The Beatles would write their lyrics down—an interesting book edited by Hunter Davies includes the handwritten drafts of Beatles songs. But there’s not a musical note in sight and not even any guitar chords. The Beatles preferred to simply remember the licks and chords they played. Paul McCartney created his guitar part to “Yesterday” by tuning his guitar down a whole step, playing chord shapes from a different key and remembering what he played. Whenever there was a need for something to be written out, such as when they hired a string quartet to play on the recording of “Yesterday,” their producer George Martin, who was conservatory trained, would write out an arrangement. Playing music by ear is really the most natural way to make music. All folk traditions are handed down aurally. I’d say that the vast majority of pop musicians, rock musicians, blues musicians and folk musicians do not read music.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What is the song 'Revolution #9' from The Beatles about?
Answer: “Revolution 9” is a sound collage from the “White Album.” The composition was co-created by John Lennon, Yoko Ono and George Harrison. Lennon said he was trying to paint a picture of a revolution using sound. However, the composition isn’t really “about” anything, as there is no narrative. It’s really just about the sounds. The composition was influenced by “musique concrete,” a style created by mixing recorded sounds. “Musique concrete” began to be developed in the 1940’s and was utilized by composers such as Edgard Varese and Karlheinz Stockhausen. For “Revolution 9,” George Harrison and Ringo Starr chose sounds from EMI’s tape library, including the famous “number nine, number nine” dialog. Lennon, Harrison and Ono started with a tape for a coda to “Revolution” that had been recorded by the four Beatles. They combined that with the sounds from the library, sound effects, and tape loops of speech and recorded music. Some of the loops were played backwards. Others were manipulated with echo, distortion, stereo panning, and other effects. The resulting 8:22 track is generally regarded as the Beatles’ least popular track. However, I think it’s notable that Lennon, Ono and Harrison were able to expose tens of millions of fans to avant-garde music that they wouldn’t have otherwise been exposed to. So, that’s really what “Revolution 9” was about.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why do the Beatles' songs sound like they are in different keys or modes when they are actually in the same key?
Answer: I have no idea what the questioner is trying to ask. Let me just say that the Beatles wrote and recorded songs in nearly every major key. The only major key that they didn’t record a song in is the key of G-flat (F-sharp). The key that the Beatles used the most often was G major, with both A-major and E-major not far behind. The group also used the Mixolydian mode often, with its flatted seventh. The Beatles also wrote and recorded songs in at least one-half of the minor keys. Their most common minor key was the key of A-minor. They commonly employed both the Dorian and the Aeolian modes. The Beatles’ song catalog is filled with great variety when it comes to keys and modes.

Question: Did Paul Simon ever write a meaningful song?

The prize has since been awarded to songwriters Stevie Wonder, Paul McCartney, the late Burt Bacharach, Carole King, Billy Joel and Smokey Robinson. That’s the kind of company Paul Simon is in. Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Can you legally copy and rewrite passages from a copyrighted work if it's now in the public domain (e.g., Dracula)?
Answer: Yes. When a work’s copyright expires, it enters the public domain and the original work is no longer protected by copyright. Bram Stokers novel “Dracula” has long been in the public domain. However, you have to be careful that you use only elements from the original work and not elements from derivative works based on the original work that have appeared within the last 95 years. Those elements may well be protected by copyright. For instance, George Gershwin’s 1924 composition “Rhapsody in Blue” is now in the Public Domain. Ferde Grofe’s original arrangement for jazz band is in the public domain. However, Grofe’s 1942 version for symphony orchestra may still have copyright protection.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: In the Beatles tune, "Norwegian Wood", does the protagonist end the song by burning some of his paramour's fine wooden items from Norway in the fireplace in her absence, perhaps to warm up the house on a cold morning?
Answer: No. In my mind, there’s no question about what happens. A guy gets invited to his girl’s place. She has cheap pine wall paneling (Norwegian wood). He bides his time, waiting to sleep with her. They talk until two in the morning and then she goes to bed, leaving him to sleep in the bathtub. After she leaves early the next morning, he sets the place on fire as an act of revenge. This interpretation is consistent with what both co-writers have said. By the way, it’s not just a John Lennon song. Co-writer Paul McCartney put it at 60% Lennon and 40% him. In fact, McCartney took credit for the very idea of setting the Norwegian wood on fire. “I burned the fucking place down as an act of revenge and then we left it there and went into the instrumental,” Paul said in his 1997 authorized biography “Many Years from Now.” McCartney called the song “funny” in a 1965 interview and described it as “tongue in cheek.” But that’s Paul McCartney—the same guy who also wrote “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer.” Lennon said he had no idea where the title “Norwegian Wood” came from. But McCartney also took credit for the title, inspired by the cheap pine wall paneling that was in vogue then in London and was in his girlfriend Jane Asher’s home. The recording is notable for at least three other reasons: First, it popularized the use the Indian stringed instrument the Sitar in rock music. Second, there was no drum set on the recording, just tambourine, maracas and finger cymbals. Third, the song clocks in at a very short 2:05.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: What happens if we don't register our book with the U.S. Copyright Office in time? Is it possible to get a copyright after the fact?
Answer: Copyright registration is not the same as “getting a copyright.” A work is copyrighted by an author the moment the work is fixed in a tangible form. A book is copyrighted the moment a manuscript is created or the book is printed. Copyright registration is a legal formality that creates a public record of the copyright and offers certain benefits to the author. For example, an author cannot file a copyright registration suit against someone unless the author’s copyright has first been registered. However, there is no deadline for registration. A work can be registered at any time.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Which Beatle received the highest royalty payments? Why was this so important to him/them financially speaking?
Answer: The answer is: None. John, Paul, George and Ringo split all record royalties, income from live performances and income from acting in motion pictures equally. They all received the same amount. Music publishing revenues were accounted for separately. Lennon and McCartney, having been credited with co-writing 160 Beatles songs made the most. George Harrison, credited for 22 Beatles songs, got significantly less and Ringo Starr, credited for 2+ Beatles songs, got the least. Lennon and McCartney got equal royalty payments from Northern Songs, then, when the catalog changed hands, from ATV Music, then Sony/ATV Music Publishing and now from Sony Music Publishing. No matter who was the principal songwriter on a song, the two split the copyrights equally and received identical royalty payments. The two split the royalties to “Yesterday” equally, even though McCartney wrote and recorded the song by himself without any other Beatles participation. Today, Lennon/McCartney compositions are still split equally. John’s portion of the royalties goes to Yoko Ono, Sean Lennon and Julian Lennon. Those three do NOT share the royalties equally.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: Why did The Beatles break up? Why were there no solo albums by any of them for so long?
Answer: Actually, the solo albums were immediate. All four of The Beatles released solo projects the same year that the band broke up. One of the solo albums was released BEFORE the group officially broke up and two were released before the final Beatles album. “Abbey Road,” the last album the band recorded, was released on Sept. 26, 1969. “Let It Be,” recorded before “Abbey Road” but delayed by Phil Spector’s production, was released on May 8, 1970. I count the official break-up date of the group as April 10, 1970. That’s the day Paul McCartney announced that he was leaving the Beatles. His solo album, “McCartney,” was released a week later on April 17, 1970, before “Let it Be.” Ringo’s solo album, “Sentimental Journey,” had already been released on March 27, 1970. George Harrison released “All Things Must Pass” on Nov. 27, 1970. John Lennon was the last one with a solo album. “John Lennon/Plastic Ono Band” was released on Dec. 11, 1970. As for “why did the Beatles break up?”—well, that’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? I say the Beatles broke up because of artistic and personal differences. They simply grew apart musically and personally. That may seem too simple, but that’s the reason.

Name: Todd Lowry
Question: If you went back in a time machine and visited the Beatles in 1963 and played them their recordings of "Helter Skelter" and "Yer Blues", telling them that those were songs they would create in 5 years, do you think they would like them?
Answer: The 1963 Beatles may well have liked the 1968 songs, but the newer songs would have sounded strange to them. And I don’t think the group would have understood how they got from their 1963 selves to the 1968 ones. In 1963, the Beatles were still basically a pub band. They made an album that year, and they had some success in Great Britain, but they had yet to visit and to eventually conquer America. The group’s standard fare in 1963 included originals such as the rock and roll “I Saw Her Standing There” and the Roy Orbison-inspired “Please Please Me.” They also played plenty of covers of songs by Chuck Berry (“Roll Over Beethoven”), Little Richard (“Long Tall Sally”) and The Top Notes (“Twist and Shout”). The 1963 Beatles couldn’t possibly have anticipated Beatlemania, the radical personal changes they went through, their growing drug use, psychedelia, the trip to India, the changes in the culture, etc. Paul McCartney’s goal on “Helter Skelter” was to create as loud and distorted a rock and roll sound as possible. He succeeded quite brilliantly. The song anticipates both heavy metal and punk. John Lennon’s goal on “Yer Blues” was to write a blues that parodied the British musician’s obsession with American blues. He, too, succeeded quite well. The 1963 Beatles may have found both songs confusing. Neither song was in a style that the group played in 1963. The 1963 Beatles would probably have also been confused by other songs on 1968’s “The White Album.” For example. they would have found the lush strings and orchestration on “Good Night” rather odd. One of the group’s biggest innovations in 1965 was to add strings and orchestrations to their rock and roll sound. The 1963 Beatles may have also been confused by the complexity of “Happiness is a Warm Gun.” There’s no telling what they may have thought of “Revolution 9.”

Question: Do you think "Imagine" by John Lennon is a better song than "Give Peace A Chance"? Why or why not?
Answer: “Give Peace A Chance” gets some points for being recorded with only two acoustic guitars (played by Lennon and Tommy Smothers) and sung by mostly amateurs (Timothy Leary, Allen Ginsberg, etc.) in a hotel room (Room 1472 of Queen Elizabeth’s Hotel) in Montreal. It did pretty well for what’s little more than a ten-note melodic theme on the words “All we are saying is give peace a chance.” I’ve never been able to understand much else that Lennon chanted on the recording. But “Imagine” covers more ground and works in a lot more ways. “Give Peace a Chance” is an anti-war song. “Imagine” manages to question war and nationalism and religion and materialism, all in a single song. “Give Peace” is upbeat and works for any peace rally. But “Imagine” has a nice melody and chords, has a standard song structure and can be enjoyed instrumentally and musically. Emotionally, it can be either optimistic or wistful. “Imagine” has been used for a wide variety of ceremonies—Opening or Closing ceremonies for the Olympics, New Year’s Eve in Times Square, Concerts for Peace, Concerts to relieve hunger, UNICEF, the United Nations, etc. It’s perfect for events following national tragedies or for funerals of statesmen and other important people. Thus, I’d say that “Imagine” is a bit more flexible and useful than “Give Peace a Chance.” I’d never argue that one was “better than” the other. They’re both important anthems that haven’t gone out of style in more than 50 years.

Question: Can you give an example of a copyright notice?
Answer: Section 401 of The Copyright Act lists the form of a copyright notice as the following three elements: Thus, here is the standard form for a copyright notice: Copyright (c) 2023 by Todd Lowry The notice is often followed by legal jargon, such as “All rights reserved.” Or “no part of this publication may be reproduced or transmitted in any form or by any means without the prior written permission of the copyright owner.” Essentially, all such jargon is extraneous. The notice should be in a “reasonable place.” In sheet music, the notice is usually at the bottom of the first page. In a book, the notice is usually on the page following the title page. Question: Do classical pianists use the pedal when they play? If so, why? If not, why not?
Answer: The standard piano has THREE pedals and the classical pianist uses them all. In fact, any pianist, in any musical genre, uses, at minimum, the left and right pedals, usually called the soft pedal and the sustain pedal. Rubenstein said that pedaling was “the soul of the piano.” That’s how important it is. It’s impossible to play the piano to its full potential without using the pedals. The right pedal, known as the sustain pedal (also called the damper pedal), is the one that pianists use the most. It raises the dampers off the strings so that they keep vibrating after the player releases the key. It’s used to connect notes in a smooth, legato manner. It also creates a rich tonal quality. Amateur pianists often use it too much, creating a muddy sound. The left pedal is the soft pedal. When depressed, it creates a softer, more ethereal sound. I use it almost as often as the sustain pedal. All acoustic pianos have, at minimum, those two pedals. Many also have a middle pedal, called the sostenuto pedal. The sostenuto pedal sustains selected notes. Without going into detail, its function is useful to more advanced pianists. Sometimes you’ll come across a piano that has a middle pedal with a different purpose, such as one that mutes the piano, so that one can practice without making much sound. Almost all portable electronic keyboards that are common today come with a single pedal that one plugs into the back of the keyboard. That pedal is the basic equivalent of the sustain pedal. When learning to play the piano, pedal technique is important. There are many issues—reading classical composers’ pedaling notations, when to depress and release the pedal, using techniques such as 1/2 pedaling, etc. These things must be practiced just like practicing the notes on the keys.

Question: How do you split royalties in a song writing/publishing agreement between two people?
Answer: In a collaboration between two writers, the two writers can agree to any percentages they like and put it in writing to make it binding. Generally, words are considered 50% of a song and music is considered 50%. Thus, writing teams that consist of a lyricist and a composer often simply split it 50/50. If one writer writes only words and the other writes words and music, then the split might be more like 75/25 or 60/40, in favor of the music AND words person. In the 20th Century, songwriters were usually either solo writers (like Irving Berline or Cole Porter) or composer/lyricist duos, like George and Ira Gershwin, Rodgers and Hart, Rodgers and Hammerstein, Leiber and Stoller, Bacharach and David, Elton John and Bernie Taupin, etc. Nowadays, it’s common to see everyone who had something to do with the song, or the initial recording of the song, given writing credit. Question: Who was the famous pianist that did not play with his fingers, but instead used his entire palm on the keys?
Answer: First, I do not know of any famous pianist who “did not play with his fingers.” I think that every pianist plays primarily with his fingers, even if the pianist uses other techniques. However, when the questioner speaks of one who “used his entire palm on the keys,” it seems to me that the questioner is talking about a pianist who uses what are called “extended piano techniques.” It could be a reference to any number of people, in various genres of music, including rock, blues, boogie-woogie, jazz and classical music. Perhaps the questioner is thinking of Jerry Lee Lewis, the great rock and roll pianist, who performed glides on the piano (glissandos), often produced tone clusters, and sometimes played with his feet or even sat on the keyboard. Or perhaps the questioner is referring to someone like Henry Cowell, a 20th Century American composer, who introduced the words “tone cluster” to piano music. He described a cluster as an aggregate of all the notes within an octave or more. In his compositions, he sometimes called for playing tone clusters on the piano with the palm of the hand. Boogie-Woogie pianists, such as Meade Lux Lewis, often played dissonant tone clusters in the right hand. In any case, such techniques are generally called “extended techniques” on the piano. So let me say a bit about the extended piano techniques that are available and common. Jerry Lee Lewis was a singer/songwriter/pianist who was one of the pioneers of rock music. The Louisiana native had huge hits in the 1950’s such as “Great Balls of Fire.” His nickname was “The Killer.” His performances were wild, frenetic and often over the top. Lewis‘s piano style was inspired by boogie-woogie piano playing. Boogie-woogie is a two-handed style that was prevalent in the 1930’s that requires a great deal of hand independence and technique. One of the techniques Lewis used was the GLISSANDO (Italian for “glide”). A glissando is a glide across one or two or three or more octaves of keys. In “Great Balls of Fire” Lewis used the glissando almost compulsively. An ascending glissando is normally performed with the right hand by placing the nail of one’s right middle finger on the keys (so you turn your hand over). Being careful not to damage your cuticle, you slide your whole hand upwards, keeping the middle finger depressed on the keys. The result should sound like a glide upwards. To glissando downwards, place the back of your right thumb on a key and then slide downward, keeping your thumb on the key. You can also use your left hand. Use the back of your left middle finger to slide down and use the back of your left thumb to slide up. A glissando is notated by a wavy line from the approximate starting note to the approximate ending note on the staff. Another person who the questioner could be referring to is Henry Cowell, a composer and pianist who introduced the idea of tone clusters in music in the mid 20th century. Cowell was known to play such clusters in several ways—such as with the palm of his hand. Other times he’d use an aid to play clusters, such as a straight-edge ruler or yardstick. He’d place the yardstick on the keyboard and depress it, playing clusters of all the white keys or all the black keys in the span of three feet. There are a number of other extended techniques that can be used. For example, the great jazz pianist Oscar Peterson often played the INSIDE of the piano. He’d form a chord shape with his left hand on the keyboard and he’d lean into the open grand piano and strum the strings with his right hand (with the nail of the middle finger). This is a great effect in itself, but it’s particularly effective when one plays chords. When one forms the chord shapes with the left hand, the dampers on the strings are raised, so that when one strums the strings, the notes of the chord that is formed are played. Another extended technique is the technique of the “prepared piano,” as developed by composer John Cage. Entire books are available about that. Extended techniques on the piano are used in rock music, blues, boogie-woogie, jazz and classical music. So, I still can’t name, for certain, the pianist the questioner is referring to, because extended techniques are used in many genres.

Question: Which Beatle played the violin on songs like "Eleanor Rigby" and "A Day In The Life"? What other instruments did they play besides the violin and guitar?

Question: Was the song "The long and winding road" written by Paul as a farewell and elegy to The Beatles, or was John correct in believing it was about The wizard of Oz?

Question: Why is "The Wizard of Oz" in the public domain while "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" is not? Who owns the rights to those stories in the United States?
Answer: Both “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” by Lewis Carroll and “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz” by L. Frank Baum have long been in the public domain. Both books are free to be used without restrictions. Alice in Wonderland was published in 1865. The Wizard of Oz was published in 1900. In the U.S., anything published prior to 1927 is in the public domain. However, the movie “The Wizard of Oz,” which was released in 1939, is NOT in the public domain and will be protected by copyright for another 12 years. The well-known movie versions of Alice in Wonderland, whether by Disney, Tim Burton or others, are also protected by copyright. When using a Public Domain writing, it’s necessary to distinguish between the original writing and a derivative work based on the original which has its own copyright.

Question: Do people own copyrights on guitar names/models and such like Les Paul or Stratocaster, etc.?
Answer: No. It’s not copyright protection. Copyright protection is given to original works of authorship in such categories as writing, musical compositions, choreography, art and sculpture, motion pictures, and sound recordings. The form of intellectual property that protects guitar names, guitar models, guitar shapes and the like, is Trademark law. Trademark law protects brand names and logos for goods and services. The Fender Musical Instrument Corporation owns many trade names, such as “Telecaster” and “Stratocaster.” In addition, it owns the “Fender” name. Gibson Brands, Inc. owns multiple trade names, like “Les Paul” and “SG.” And, of course, it owns the name “Gibson.” Gibson even has trademark applications for the distinctive shapes of several of its guitar models, such as The Flying V, The Les Paul, the SG and others. The United States government agency that deals with trademarks is the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, with 12,579 employees. The U.S. Copyright Office is much smaller, with 440 employees.

Question: What are the legalities of covers? If a cover is made without permission from the original artist, can the artist sue?
Answer: Cover recordings are legitimized by the U.S. Copyright Act, Section 115. That section says that when a song is recorded and distributed in the U.S., ANY OTHER PERSON can then record the song and distribute recordings. It’s called a COMPULSORY LICENSE. That means that the copyright owner CANNOT stop the person from recording a cover. And the person recording the cover doesn’t need any permission from the copyright owner. Here are the only caveats: 1. The person who records the cover must pay the copyright owner the statutory mechanical license rate for each copy sold. That rate is 9.1 cents per song, per copy sold. 2. the person who records the cover must serve notice on the copyright owner. It must be in writing. Royalty payments must be made every month. 3. The person making the cover CANNOT change the basic melody or the fundamental character of the song. For that the person does need the permission of the copyright owner. Thus, cover recordings are not only legal, they are encouraged by the provisions of the Copyright Act.

Question: Do experienced pianists practice differently compared to those who are just beginning?
Answer: Of course. First, when is the time that practice occurs? Beginners are encouraged to have a regular practice time, such as shortly after school lets out for the day. That also happens to be the best time to teach lessons. Experienced pianists who have teaching careers, often have to find time to practice. One of my activities involves spending time at elementary schools during school hours. As a result, I practice a lot in the early morning and fairly late at night. Second, what is the length of practice? I find that few beginners practice more than an hour a day. Experienced pianists, usually spend several hours a day practicing and can sometimes spend 6, 8, or 10 hours a day practicing. Third, what is the content of practice? Beginner’s practice routines are generally set by their instructors. Beginners may balance learning repertoire, with learning theory, technical exercises (such as scales) and other things. Experienced pianists work in a more intuitive manner. They have to be more goal oriented. If they have an imminent performance approaching, they may practice a single piece over and over. I once spent 10 hours straight practicing a single page of a Rachmaninoff prelude. That was the best use of my time in that particular situation. Another consideration is technical exercises. Beginners are encouraged to practice scales and the like. I rarely practice such things. How many pieces will you ever play that have scales in octaves or two-handed arpeggios in them? When beginning a new piece, an experienced player can spend hours initially just fingering a piece. Fingering for beginners is something that’s generally provided by the instructor. I think it’s useful for beginners to play a piece with the beat of a metronome to develop a better sense of rhythm and flow. However, other than finding a metronome marking for a piece, I don’t use metronomes much. Here are a couple more practice strategies that are valuable for a beginning pianist but not necessarily for an experienced pianist: Playing one hand at a time, slowing down a passage and playing it very slowly, and practicing the hard parts of a particular piece rather than going over the easy parts.

Question: Do people think that Paul McCartney's vocal range was as good as John Lennon's?
Answer: I’m sure that most casual fans think that Paul McCartney had a larger vocal range than John Lennon. I thought that before I actually looked at the facts. The facts say that Lennon’s vocal range was slightly larger than McCartney’s. A vocal range is the range of musically useful pitches that a person can sing from the lowest to the highest. You take the lowest note a singer can sing and you find the highest note the singer can sing. The distance between those pitches is the singer’s vocal range. Paul McCartney’s lowest note on record was a B2 (“And I Love Her”). His highest note on record is F5 (“Maybe I’m Amazed”). That’s a range of two octaves and a tritone. John Lennon’s lowest note was G2 (The “Mother Superior jumped the gun” part in “Happiness is a Warm Gun”). His highest note was the D5 he sang in “Happiness” near the end on the word “gun”. That’s a range of two octaves and a 5th, a range 1/2 step larger than McCartney’s. McCartney sings HIGHER—by a minor third. But Lennon had more low end notes. John Lennon’s vocal range is larger than McCartney’s. It’s possible that I missed a song or songs that demonstrate otherwise. But the examples I’ve listed clearly demonstrate that Lennon had a larger vocal range.

Question: What is the Bee Gees' greatest claim to fame in copyright law?
Answer: Selle v. Gibb, 1984, was a landmark music copyright infringement case. It stands for the legal rule that copying must be proved by showing TWO things: 1. Substantial similarity between the original song and the alleged infringing song; and 2. The infringer had access to the original song. Ronald Selle, an Illinois resident, wrote a song entitled “Let it End” in 1975. He was issued a copyright registration certificate in the same year. In 1978, Selle heard the Bee Gee’s “How Deep Is Your Love” and he recognized the song as his melody, with different words. Selle sued Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb for copyright infringement. Selle based his case on the doctrine of “substantial similarity.“ He showed how 16 bars in his composition and 16 bars in “How Deep Is Your Love” were strikingly similar. However, he offered no proof of access—he didn’t show that the Bee Gees had actually heard his song. The jury returned a verdict in favor of Selle. But the trial judge granted the defendant’s motion for a judgement notwithstanding the verdict. The judge said that the jury’s verdict went against the evidence. The case was appealed and the appeals court upheld the judge’s decision. Essentially, Selle did not prove one of the elements of copyright infringement. The plaintiff must prove that the infringer had access to his song. Access means that the defendant actually heard the song. This was not proven here. The Bee Gees were not liable for Copyright infringment.

Question: What is overdubbing? Did The Beatles use overdubbing when recording songs? If so, how was it done? Did they have multiple tracks on which to record simultaneously (e.g., bass and drums)?
Answer: Overdubbing is a technique in audio recording in which audio tracks that have already been recorded are played back and other tracks are played along and recorded to go with them. The Beatles used overdubbing extensively. The band’s first two albums, “Please Please Me” and “With the Beatles” were recorded essentially as a live performance. The Beatles set up and played in the studio as they did in a live gig. But with the introduction of four-track recording machines in 1963, the Beatles were able to build up recordings layer by layer and track by track. Later, in 1968, eight-track machines became available. The Beatles used overdubbing for many reasons. First, they liked the sound of double tracking the lead vocals to make them stronger and thicker. This was initially done by singing an identical vocal part with the original vocal part. Eventually, the process was automated—it was turned into Artificial Double Tracking. Second, the Beatles often played more than one instrument on a recording. For instance, Paul McCartney would play a piano part on the basic track. Then later he would overdub the bass part. Then, later he would add his own voice in vocal harmony. All the Beatles were multi-instrumentalists and they often played many parts. Third, the Beatles began to add more and more orchestral instruments. This began with the string quartet in “Yesterday,” which was overdubbed onto the recording of Paul singing and playing his acoustic guitar. It became fairly routine for the Beatles to have orchestral instruments overdubbed. Fourth, they began to use samples —like the BBC broadcast recording of “King Lear” that was mixed into “I Am the Walrus.” Or the recordings of calliope and steam organ that were mixed into “For the Benefit of Mr. Kite.” Fifth, the Beatles began to layer vocals. They were excellent at singing three-part harmonies. And it became more common for them to double or triple all the voices—think of the song “Because” and its beautifully layered vocals. Sixth, the Beatles began to use experimental tape processes—like playing tapes backwards and using tape loops Overdubbing was a common process in the recording studio for the Beatles.

Question: How did The Beatles make their songs sound different from each other using only four chords?

Most of those songs are straight-ahead rockers such as “I Saw Her Standing There,” “I’m Down” and “One After 909.” Generally, the Beatles used a far more interesting harmonic palette than four chords. However, in the studio, they could make anything sound interesting. Their 1966 song “Tomorrow Never Knows” has the most limited harmonic palette they ever used—two chords, C and Bb/C. Yet, that song sounds like no other song in the history of rock music. It used an Indian-inspired underpinning of tambura and sitar, a C mixolydian scale, a unique drum beat, tape loops prepared by every member of the band, Lennon’s voice fed through a Leslie speaker, backwards guitar parts, the Mellotron and many other studio effects. So, the Beatles rarely used as few as four chords. But when they wanted to, they made things sound interesting through means other than chord progressions.

Question: Are there any defenses to copyright infringement?
Answer: I was involved in a case in which one of the most famous songwriters in the world was accused of copying a song by a songwriter who was virtually an unknown. For such a plaintiff to prove that someone copied his musical composition or song, the plaintiff must prove three things: 2. That the defendant had “access” to the song. The plaintiff must prove that the defendant heard the song. 3. That the defendant’s song is so “substantially similar” to the plaintiff’s song, it had to have been copied. Defenses, then, include: 1. The plaintiff doesn’t have a legitimate copyright to the song. 2. The defendant never had access to the plaintiff’s song— the song was not well-known or it was unpublished. 3. The similarity to the defendant’s song doesn’t rise to “substantial similarity.” Another defense is to claim that the so-called infringing musical passages are in the public domain. Believe it or not, this is a very popular defense. Essentially the defendant is saying,” I didn’t copy your song. I copied from older, public domain sources and that’s okay.”

Question: Did all four members of The Beatles receive equal songwriting credits, or did some get more than others depending on how much they contributed to a song musically?
Answer: Here’s how the Beatles songwriting credits worked. John Lennon and Paul McCartney are credited with writing 160 of the more than 200 songs the Beatles recorded on their official albums. George Harrison is credited with writing 22 Beatles songs. Ringo Starr is credited with writing 2 Beatles songs. Plus the Beatles recorded 23 covers. As far as Lennon and McCartney go, the two friends made a pact when they were teenagers that any songs they wrote for the band, whether they were written together or apart, would be credited to the two of them—Lennon and McCartney. As such, they each own 50% of the writer’s share of Lennon/McCartney songs. They share 50/50 all songwriting royalties, no matter what each’s individual contribution to the song was. (Lennon’s songwriting royalties go to Yoko Ono.) Of the 160 Beatles songs they wrote, only 18 are considered 50/50 collaborations. For the others, Beatles experts have designated a “principal songwriter” for each song. The principal songwriter essentially came up with the song idea and wrote the main body of the song, sometimes with the other’s help, editing and encouragement. The principal songwriter generally sang lead on the songs that he was the principal songwriter for. Thus, there are “John songs” and there are “Paul songs.” John songs: Please Please Me, Help!, Ticket to Ride, Strawberry Fields Forever, Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds, and I Am the Walrus. Paul songs: Love Me Do, Can’t Buy Me Love, Eight Days a Week, Let it Be, Penny Lane and Hey Jude. Ringo played drums on all the recordings and George played lead guitar and often sang. George Martin arranged all the orchestral parts that are on Beatles records. None of the three ever received any songwriting credit for any Lennon/McCartney songs. That’s because they didn’t write the words or the melodies for the songs. In traditional songwriting, the words and the tune are considered the essence of a pop song. Playing drums or lead guitar on the recordings, or producing and arranging the recordings, does not constitute songwriting.

Question: Who was a better pianist, Oscar Peterson or Thelonious Monk?
Answer: Oscar Peterson had more technical chops than just about any other jazz pianist, except Art Tatum. Yet, Peterson always incorporated a contagiously swinging beat, vast harmonic richness and an element of earthy blues. He was one of the most popular jazz pianists for about 50 years. When I watch videos of Thelonious Monk playing, I am struck by his completely unorthodox piano technique. His touch was harsh and percussive. He played with flat fingers. He attacked the piano. He unintentionally hit wrong notes with his large fingers that gave the impression of someone playing the piano while wearing work gloves. It was the opposite of smooth or fluid. Furthermore, Monk would abruptly stand up in the middle of a set and take a 20-minute walk. It seems to me that Monk’s importance is more as a composer than as a pianist. I think I’d have to say that Oscar Peterson was a better pianist than Monk, at least in a technical sense. But then I’d have to admit that Monk remains more influential than Peterson, both as a composer AND AS A PIANIST.

Question: Do you think that "Imagine" by John Lennon was a successful song? Why or why not?
Answer: “Imagine” is unbelievably successful as a song. Successful in the sense that the song, by John Lennon and Yoko Ono, encourages listeners to think about war, hunger and religion in a respectful and calm way. It makes a plea for peace in the world that is clear and unwavering. The song generally strikes the right note of sincerity and optimism. “Imagine” has become one of the most recognizable pop songs in the world. In times of trouble and grief, it’s the number one song that people turn to for inspiration and solace. It’s been used at countless Olympics opening and closing ceremonies, at Times Square New Year’s Eve Celebrations, at funerals for dignitaries, at memorial concerts and at concerts to raise money and awareness for Peace. It’s been played at the Vatican, at the U.N. and at the White House. It’s a subversive song—the song questions the very nature of religion, of countries and of nationalism. Lennon married instrumental music that was simple and conventional with his radical message. “Imagine” is so calm musically, that both the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Pope have used it in public ceremonies. It’s a successful song because it communicates what Lennon wanted it to communicate.

Question: What are the differences between Paul McCartney and John Lennon's voices? Which one had a better range/pitch, and which one sounded better live with The Beatles?
Answer: John Lennon and Paul McCartney were each outstanding vocalists, both as soloists and as harmony singers in the band. Both could sing in a variety of styles. They were each adept at singing ballads. Think of Paul on “Blackbird” and John on “Julia.” Both could really turn on the rock and roll when they wanted to. Think of Paul on “Oh! Darling” and John on “Twist and Shout.” They each had extraordinarily large ranges. John’s range was slightly larger, because had more low range than Paul. Paul could sing somewhat higher than John and he sounded beautiful in his upper range. Unbelievably, John once demonstrated his entire range in one song, “Happiness is a Warm Gun.” He used a range of two octaves and a fifth on that song. Paul had a range almost as large, at two octaves and an augmented 4th. John sang with confidence and passion, Paul with control and precision. Rolling Stone magazine ranks Paul as #11 on the list of greatest vocalists and John as #5. Whether you agree with that or not, there’s no question that both were among the greatest rock singers of all time.

Question: What is the meaning of John Lennon's song "I am the Walrus"? How does it relate to his music and life?
Answer: In “Walrus,” Lennon intentionally wrote words that were obscure and had no real meaning. He was having a laugh with listeners who took his lyrics too seriously. Lennon had previously written the two books “In His Own Write” and “A Spaniard in the Works,” which were madcap, inspired nonsense—wild and preposterous. That’s like the lyrics here. Lennon was also inspired by the Lewis Carroll poem, “The Walrus and the Carpenter” and by his own personal use of LSD at the time.

Question: Which band members of The Beatles could actually play their instruments?
Answer: All four of the Beatles were excellent on their respective instruments. Generally, each one is usually considered to be in the Top Ten of all time for their instruments. There’s no question about McCartney on bass or Starr on drums. John Lennon was one of the greatest rhythm guitarists ever. The entire sound of the early Beatles was built around Lennon’s solid rhythm guitar. And George Harrison developed into one of the world’s greatest lead guitarists. His mature sound—as evidenced on “Abbey Road”—is one of the most recognizable lead guitar sounds there’s ever been. Harrison played guitar solos that were so melodic and well-structured that, to this day, casual Beatles fans can sing entire solos note for note. (See, for instance, his solo on “Something.”) In addition, BOTH Lennon and McCartney are considered to be among the Top Rock Pianists. The Beatles were, first and foremost, great musicians. Everything else followed from that fact.
